Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36 on behalf of a number of Kamloops residents who are dismayed that the Government is changing the Unemployment Insurance Act to require that financing for training be taken from unemployment insurance funds.
June 20, 1989

They are also concerned because this means that higher premiums will have to be paid by employees as well as employers. I do not think we have seen the end of the impact that this change will have on the small business community of the country. The petitioners are calling upon the Government to come to its senses and back off from this regressive step.

Mr. Speaker, I have another petition signed by residents of Kamloops, British Columbia, who point out their concern regarding the Government's support for the growing militarization of our economy. They go on at some length to point out the details of their concern that we seem to be moving our economy to one which is tied more closely to the American military complex.
The petitioners call upon the Government to back off from this involvement and to encourage the diversion of military spending to socially important areas which create jobs while strengthening Canada's commitment to peace.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present petitions on behalf of approximately 18,000 Canadians. These 18,000 Canadians recognize that the Carmanah Valley, approximately mid-way along the West Coast Trail, is carpeted with an ancient forest of cedar, hemlock and Sitka spruce, the spruce especially being outstanding examples of their species including the tallest in the world and the tallest known tree in Canada, a tree 312 feet, taller than a 30-storey building or the Parliament Buildings.
The petitioners submit that in order to preserve the Sitka spruce ecology in perpetuity their entire natural forest valley habitat must be protected, for logging in the watershed will increase run-off erosion and open up the tall trees to the force of the wind which inevitably causes the ancient trees to be blown down.
The petitioners therefore ask that a full assessment of the ecological significance of the Carmanah Valley be undertaken by Environment Canada, including the merits and values as a tourist attraction with extended trails from the West Coast Trail and that pending the results of these studies the federal Government enter into negotiations with the provincial Government to protect and preserve the entire valley as an addition to the Pacific Rim National Park.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (for the Minister of the Environment) moved
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: that Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity today to speak on second reading of Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. This Bill will correct an unfortunate drafting error which is in fact holding up Canada's participation in the fight to protect the ozone layer.
As we all know, CEPA became law on June 30, 1988. That legislation was designed to protect the health and environment of Canadians. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act provides the legislative basis for coming to terms with the complex issues of air and water pollution, toxic substances management, waste disposal, acid rain and climate warming.
The new Act embodies an ecosystem vision of environmental protection. It addresses pollution problems on land, in water and through all layers of the atmosphere. The Act recognizes that ecosystems extend beyond national borders. It provides the legislative basis to enable us to control international environmental degradation through restrictions on the import and export of dangerous substances and through the regulation of Canadian sources of transboundaiy air pollution.
The Act deals with organic and inorganic substances, the products of biotechnology, emissions, effluence and wastes. It gives the Government the authority to impose strict controls at each stage of a toxic substance's life cycle.
The Act is designed to protect against environmental contamination from toxic substances. According to CEPA, a substance is toxic if it threatens human health or the environment. The Act adopts a two-pronged approach to managing toxic substances. First, the regulating of those substances now in the Canadian marketplace, many of which we know little about. Second, controlling the introduction of substances that are new to Canada.
Once a substance is found to be toxic, an order is made to add this substance to Schedule I of the Act. The order is effective on the date a regulation pertaining to the substance takes effect. Regulations may address any aspect of the life cycle of a substance, including manufacture and import, storage, handling, packaging, distribution, transportation, sale, use, release and disposal.
The Canadian Environmental Protection Act builds on earlier environmental statutes. These include, among others, the Clean Air Act, the Ocean Dumping Control Act and the Environmental Contaminants Act.
CEPA incorporated the various regulations developed under these laws; regulations dealing with lead, mercury, vinyl chloride, and asbestos in air emissions; with phosphorous in detergents; with lead in gasoline; with PCBs, mercury and mirex. These regulations were intended to be applied upon promulgation of the Act on June 30, 1988 in accordance with the CEPA enforcement and compliance policy.
At the same time, many of the substances dealt with in the regulations were included on the list of toxic substances in Schedule I to the Act.
There are nine such substances, PCBs, mirex, polybro-minated biphenyls, CFCs, polychlorinated terphenyls, asbestos, lead, mercury and vinyl chloride.
June 20, 1989

It is in this process of listing, on Schedule I, substances found to be toxic which concerns us here today.
To be clear, Schedule I identifies those substances which can contaminate the environment and thus should be controlled. Listing a substance allows us to strengthen the earlier regulatory requirements and/or develop further controls as necessary.
On that basis, the Government ratified, within hours of the promulgation of CEPA, the so-called Montreal protocol for the protection of the ozone layer. On that basis as well, the Government announced on February 20, 1989, a national program to eliminate CFCs from Canada within the next 10 years.
Unfortunately, the basis for those actions has been compromised. According to our legal advice, the inclusion of a list of toxic substances in Schedule I in CEPA, as passed, was not appropriate. The Act requires that substances be added to the Schedule only through an order of the Governor in Council. Orders are based on evidence of the toxic effects of the substance in question. They take effect once regulations are developed. Thus, the nine substances, to which I have already referred, because of the absence of such an order, probably had no legitimacy.
This created several dilemmas, not the least of which was a regulatory hiatus, where the current regulations dealing with the nine substances in question may have been unenforceable.
Faced with this advice, the Government took immediate steps to address this situation. Earlier this spring, the Government republished the regulations in the form of interim orders under CEPA. By virtue of Section 35, interim orders have the effect of a regulation but for a lifespan of only two years.
The Government also reviewed the various options for correcting the list of toxic substances and, in particular, ensuring that we could move ahead to meet our national and global obligations to further control CFCs.
The most obvious option was to complete an assessment of the environmental and health impacts of each of the nine substances. Using existing scientific data, both Canadian and international, the Government could prepare assessment reports, publish summaries of these findings, consult with various stakeholders and develop the appropriate recommendations for a Governor in Council order. We could then publish regulations for
Environmental Protection
comments. The difficulty with this approach was and is its timing. We are already seized with assessing 44 existing substances recommended as priorities by an independent advisory panel. We are also completing our assessment work done on dioxins and furans. We are assessing benzine, waste oils and polyaromatic hydrocarbons among others.
We hope to finalize the assessments of at least nine substances over the next few months and to publish regulatory controls as appropriate.
Quite frankly, we would prefer to concentrate our efforts on evaluating the new or the unknown, rather than reinventing the wheel on those substances already deemed to be toxic enough to justify regulation under earlier laws.
Our preferred solution is the one presented here today, that of amending the legislation to modify the effective date of an order adding substances to the Schedule, in effect, removing the link to the publication of regulations. This change, once approved, would allow the Governor in Council to make an order creating the list of toxic substances and thereby providing a basis for the regulations in effect prior to June, 1988, under earlier legislation and for any new regulations relative to the nine substances which I have already identified.
Quick consideration of Bill C-22 will allow us to persevere in our efforts to develop controls for additional substances. Quick consideration of Bill C-22 will also allow us to meet the July 1, 1989 international deadline for action to protect the ozone layer.
Many of us, and perhaps most of us, in this House share the growing concern about the changes taking place in the gases which make up the earth's atmosphere. In particular, we are monitoring the disappearance of the ozone layer which protects the earth from the impact of the ultraviolet rays of the sun. The international scientific community has concluded that CFCs, a synthetic chemical developed in the 1930s, are responsible for modifying the ozone layer.
Canada acted in the mid 1970s to reduce the use of CFCs. Using the formal Environmental Contaminants Act, Canada developed regulations controlling the import, use and manufacture of CFCs. As of June 30,1988, those regulations were to have been transferred and applied under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. CFCs were included on the list of toxic substances under the Act.

June 20,1989
Environmental Protection
We now need to move ahead and strengthen our control of CFCs and in fact eliminate them altogether. As I have described, the legislative basis for these actions has been questioned. We propose, through Bill C-22, to correct that.
This Government's commitment to protecting the well-being of this planet is strong. We believe in strong domestic action to control toxic contamination. We believe also in the need for strong international action. The fight against the depletion of the ozone layer is a case in point.
I ask the House, therefore, to approve Bill C-22 and to correct the legal technicality now inhibiting Canada's actions to control CFCs. Parliamentary study and approval of CEPA, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, was exemplary in terms of the co-operation and the positive contributions made by all Parties to improve the legislation. I would ask this House to continue that tradition in approving this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am a little amazed that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Clark) has not put this government foul-up in context. According to a phone call the Minister is here in Parliament. I do not know why he is not here to speak on his own legislation. On February 20 the Minister issued a major press release in which he stated:
I am tomorrow issuing draft national regulations to curb CFC use.
When the original Canadian Environmental Protection Act was introduced, it was condemned widely by environmentalists as being badly worded, bewildering, and confused.
The very wording problem that has been exposed and is now to be rectified as a result of the amendments under Bill C-22 was applauded by the then Minister of the Environment. Several groups and organizations appeared before the committee and pointed out that if the wording in the Act were not cleaned up we would see a situation where a number of specific improvements could not be applied.
What did the then Minister of the Environment have to say about that criticism? During the course of the committee hearings the then Minister, Mr. McMillan, said:
We do not have at present, under either of these bodies of law or under any others authority to control, cap or reduce production, prohibit new production facilities or control imports of ozone-depleting substances from specific countries, for example, nonparties; nor do we have the authority to control exports to Pacific countries.
We will have all those powers under CEPA if Parliament passes it as it is.
That was a statement made by the Conservative Minister of the Environment a year and a half ago when we were asked to pass the badly worded Canadian Environmental Protection Act in the House.
We now see that the Minister has recognized the folly of his own legislation and has brought forward amendments to attempt to address the specific shortcomings of the chlorofluorocarbon regulations.
In February presumably, if we take him at his word, the Minister did begin examination of the regulatory process. I cannot understand why he did not discover at that time that because of the wording of the Act we would not be able to meet our obligations under the Montreal Protocol. Our obligations under the Montreal Protocol begin in approximately 10 days. Now we are being asked in a shoddy, haphazard effort similar to the effort that was not shown, in so far as cleaning up the original wording of CEPA, to pass this new regulation change with very little involvement or assessment by the 1,800 environmental groups across this country that have a particular interest in what CFCs are doing to the ozone. In particular, the Minister is ignoring the suggestion by the Liberal Party that while we are moving to implement a cut-back in CFC use as agreed by the Montreal Protocol we should be examining the use of CFCs and their disposal in relation to refrigeration.
As we speak there are approximately one million refrigerators produced by General Electric, of which
25,000	are being produced in Canada by Cameo in Hamilton that are being repaired because of a faulty manufacturing process in relation to the CFCs. They are being drained irresponsibly and with great damage into the environment.
June 20, 1989

The Minister would have us believe that Canada is at the forefront of reduction of CFCs in the world. Yet, he brings forward an amendment which, albeit we will support because it should be supported, should have been brought in three months ago at the time when the Minister first discovered this gross error in drafting perpetrated on Parliament by his own Party.
He should have brought this amendment forward and he should have permitted a full public examination. Instead we are being told that we must pass this Bill by tomorrow or the next day because if we do not the Minister will not be able to have a press conference announcing that he has met his obligations under the Montreal Protocol. If the Minister is going to start doing and stop talking-he has been Minister for almost six month-he should start examining in greater detail the implications of the unfettered use of CFCs in relation to refrigeration. In particular, he should know that industries, private individuals, in fact anybody, can drain CFCs directly into the atmosphere at the moment with absolutely no federal regulations to govern that situation. What kind of a climate are we actually creating?

Despite the Minister's lavish comments on the Montreal Protocol, Canada is currently welcoming to its Eastern Townships second-hand refrigerators that are being off-loaded in dumps all over the place and are draining CFCs into the atmosphere, in absolute contravention of the Montreal Protocol. And the Minister was asked when he would be making changes in the regulations under the Environmental Protection Act-why isn't he introducing regulations governing CFCs in refrigerators?

The Minister has the power. Why does he not exercise it? He has the power under Section 35 of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act to determine that the absolute negligence of companies that are prepared to allow CFCs to leak into the atmosphere should be the subject of an environmental emergency. We are talking about the coolant of one million refrigerators being leaked into the atmosphere, yet the Minister of the Environment refuses to do anything. The Minister would have us believe that he is very determined to meet his obligations under the Montreal Protocol. What has the
Environmental Protection
Minister been doing since February 20? What has the Minister been doing since he stated:
I am tomorrow issuing draft regulations to curb CFC use by more than 85 per cent.
Instead at literally the twelfth hour-that is 11 days before the date of the implementation of the Montreal Protocol-we are being told we have to pass this Bill today no questions asked.
In a report Greenpeace had a few things to say yesterday about CFCs. It gave a fairly damning indictment of the activity or lack of activity of the federal Government in relation to CFCs. What Greenpeace said bears repeating. Friends of the Earth that also has a non-governmental, non-biased, objective assessment of the federal Government's environmental record today is saying that the clock is ticking in relation to the hundreds of thousands of refrigerators. The clock is ticking in relation to the fact that as a matter of public policy the Government is creating a situation where we are being asked to welcome with open arms used, broken down, and leaky refrigerators from the United States.
Surely, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act has been drafted in such a way to permit the Government to act, not only in relation to our obligations under the Montreal Protocol but in particular in relation to our obligations under the Government's much vaunted commitment to the environment.
The Government and the Minister like to say that they play a leadership role. In early May of this year the first meeting of the Parties at the Vienna Convention and the Montreal Protocol were held in Helsinki, Finland. One of the issues discussed was a rapid phase-out of CFCs. They also looked at the specific issue of how to help developing countries in reducing and eliminating their use of CFCs.
We in the have countries have created many of the problems, and we are now putting a stop to the expansion of the manufacture of things like CFCs at the same time that the have not countries are saying "hey, wait a minute. You created the problem. You put the holes in our ozone layer, and now you are telling us that we cannot have the same kind of progress in relation to our Gross National Product as you have had". The have countries have milked the earth, and now we are telling the have not countries, the Third World countries, that it is their turn to bring forward regulations. That will obviously cost money.

June 20, 1989
Environmental Protection
At that meeting in Helsinki, Mostafa Tolba, head of the United Nations Environmental Program, suggested a specific initiative which would have created an international climate fund to assist developing countries to meet their obligations imposed on them by developing countries, for the most part under treaties and agreements like the Montreal Protocol.
As a result of that conference, Norway immediately offered to spend 0.1 per cent of its Gross National Product, approximately $105 million, on the international climate fund to save the world and to give developing countries the capacity to impose regulations that we want to impose upon ourselves. Why did Canada refuse to follow Norway's lead?
Let us examine the funding for CFC regulations that were gazetted on April 22, 1989. How much has the federal Government committed to spending on efforts to combat CFCs here in Canada? Is it in the millions? Is it in the billions? Is it half a million? It is a paltry, pathetic $223,000 from a Government that until a few short weeks ago was prepared to spend $10 billion on nuclear powered submarines.
That's even less than Marcel's book.

That is right. It might be a bit more, unless the book goes into repeat copies, but that is not likely to happen. It is approximately the combined cost of the appearance of the Minister of Communications at the Oscar ceremony and the cost of his book.
In my opinion and in the opinion of the Liberal Party, the Government is not committing funding and it is in fact cutting funding to CFC reduction and other specific strategies to clean up the environment because of what it has stated.

On a number of occasions during the election campaign the Prime Minister himself stated that the environment was the Tories' No. One concern. But then you look at the amount of money allocated to meet our obligations under the Montreal Protocol and it's $233,000 annually. That's laughable, Mr. Speaker, it's practically an insult. This government was ready to spend $10 billion on nuclear submarines, but it's going to pay $233,000 to meet our obligations under the Montreal
Protocol! And now here they are urging us to pass this legislation right away, without any debate, without hearing from any groups like Friends of the Earth, who are currently busy exposing the complete bankruptcy of the federal government's environment polity. The government doesn't want to hear from Greenpeace either, which just yesterday announced that they were completely opposed to the Conservative policies, which talked a lot about the problem of CFCs but did very little.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that all this wearies the Hon. Member for Brampton (Mr. McDermid). He isn't interested in the fact that the ozone layer is in the process of being eaten away. But I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that many thousands-and even many millions-of Canadians would like to be able to breathe good Canadian air 50 years from now. They would like to be able to live in a country that was not overheating. And at the present time our own manufacture of products like chlorofluoro-carbons, for example, is destroying the atmosphere's ability to absorb distant light, Mr. Speaker. We are going to create a situation where in 75 years this planet, including Canada, will be overheated to crisis point-we are seeing that already when every summer the earth heats up another degree or two or more. We are seeing-

It is the dog days of summer. They are increasing by leaps and bounds. It has very little to do with natural climatic change but has very much to do with the damage we are inflicting on ourselves.
If the Government is really serious about a major assault on chlorofluorocarbons, it should do more than it has. It has brought amendments before us which are mere housekeeping amendments to resolve a situation the Government created for itself by asking Parliament to pass a poorly worded and indefensible amendment to the Canada Environmental Protection Act. If the Government is truly serious, it should couple these amendments with other specific initiatives relating to refrigerants and CFCs escaping into the environment on a daily basis. Frankly, I doubt that the Conservatives will move in such a direction. As far as they are concerned, the philosophy of their Party and their Government is that everything is driven by the almighty buck.
June 20, 1989

Let us go back for a moment and examine statements made by various Conservative Members at a time when we were in a position to bring forward strong and specific legislation relating to CFCs and refrigerants. The then Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake, in a debate on a motion held on March 8, 1988, had the following to say about the fact that were killing ourselves with our own CFCs:
Certainly, research is fundamental to getting environmentally safe substitutes to market. But given the potential profits, is this not an activity that would be best left to the private sector?
The private sector means companies like General Electric, a company which is right now in the process of leaking CFCs from one million refrigerators into the North American environment. If the private sector can do this cheaper and without the added expense of environmental protection laws, what incentive would there be for it to do it in a way that would be environmentally sustainable? The private sector looks for the bottom line.
Speaking of specific research, a representative of the Government of Canada, when confronted with this absolutely scandalous corporate behaviour of leaking CFCs into the environment, said that no technology exists which can actually effectively recycle CFCs. That is an absolute falsehood.
I do not have the resources of a multi-million dollar Department at my disposal. I have three people working in my office in Ottawa and two working in my office in Hamilton, and it did not take me that long to get in touch with Roger Dumais, the regional sales manager for ThermaFlo in Springfield, Massachusetts, a company with capacity to reclaim and recharge chlorofluorocar-bons. This company recycles chlorofluorocarbons from used refrigerators to other units.
Notwithstanding the Government's claim that no technology exists, the brochure of this company says that now it is easy to recycle refrigerants, protect our atmosphere and, according to the brochure, save money. This company has developed the most effective, low cost, portable CFC reclamation and charging unit on the market today. It can be used in automobiles with air conditioners, buses, trucks, room air conditioners, refrigerators, commercial chillers, and virtually any refrigeration system utilizing CFCs as a refrigerant. At the moment this very company is in discussion with companies such as General Electric, so the technology exists. How can the Minister possibly justify a statement by his own Department that
Environmental Protection
no specific technology exists to reclaim chlorofluorocarbons? That is simply false.
It is no wonder that the public confidence in the political process is undermined when we have a Minister of the Environment who is essentially the head of the Department that is spreading falsehoods about the capacity to reclaim chlorofluorocarbons.
When the Minister comes before the House, as he has by way of his Parliamentary Secretary today, and asks us to pass those specific amendments with respect to CFCs, we say yes. We want to support the Minister, even though it took him approximately three or four months to find out that his own legislation was not up to scratch. If he is to introduce specific legislation in relation to CFCs, surely he should deal with the over-all objectives of the reduction, not only in the manufacture and new production of CFCs but also in the recycling of CFCs as they are currently being used by millions of Canadians.
That is why today in committee we have suggested that in the course of approving this legislation we would like to hear from groups such as Greenpeace, the Canadian Environmental Law Association, Canadian Environmental Network, and Friends of the Earth to see what suggestions they may have to improve and ameliorate the legislation before us.
I must say again that I do not know to whom the Government is talking and with whom the Minister is consulting. He certainly does not seem to be consulting very much with environmental groups. If he had consulted with them, he would have known that according to a release which came out this morning from Friends of the Earth the technology is currently available to cut production of CFCs by over 60 per cent in three years and eliminated by 1995.
As we have stated both in committee and in the House today, the Government also has the capacity to use its emergency powers under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act to ban CFCs in aerosols, rug underpadding, and foam packaging immediately. Information note.
Issue: Amendments to Sections 33 and 34 of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
Background:
The Canadian Environmental Protection Act received Royal Assent on June 30,1988. Section 34 of the Act provides authorities to regulate toxic substances there added by order to Schedule 1, the List of Toxic Substances. The Act as passed in 1988 contains a List of Toxic Substances in Schedule 1 that were added by Parliament, not by order.
As a consequence, regulations developed under the Clean Air Act and the Environmental Contaminants Act and consolidated under CEPA were found not to be enforceable.
In addition, the current wording of S. 34 makes it impossible to develop additional regulations for the toxic substances that were listed by Parliament.
Existing regulations therefore were temporarily brought back into force by the use of Interim Orders.
Although the Act provides that Interim Orders are effective for two years or until replaced by regulations, the replacement regulations cannot be made without amending S. 34.
More importantly, Canada's commitment under the Montreal Protocol on the Protection of the Ozone Layer to Regulate Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) by July 1, 1989, cannot be met, since CFCs are already on the List of Tbxic Substances in Schedule 1.
The amendments to Sections 33 and 34 correct the wording error by removing the need for an order to be made to add a substance to the List of Toxic Substances before regulations can be made in respect to the substance.
That is what the Minister's note says.
Let me quote what the Library of Parliament has to say in its June 8,1989 note to members of the committee:
An Act to amend the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, notes on Bill C-22.
Bill C-22, which received first reading in the House of Commons on June 1, 1989, would amend sections 33 and 34 of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, (CEPA), as proclaimed into force on June 30, 1988. The Bill, composed of two clauses, can be best described as housekeeping in nature. It would remove certain anomalies found in sections 33 and 34 that pose problems in respect of the regulation of toxic substances.

June 20, 1989
Environmental Protection
In order to regulate a toxic substance under CEPA, the substance must first be placed on the List of Toxic Substances found in Schedule 1 to the Act. Section 33 currently provides for the inclusion on or deletion of a substance from this List.
A substance is added to the List by order of the Governor in Council, but the order becomes effective only when regulations affecting the substance made pursuant to section 34 of the Act come into force, (subsections 33(1) and 33(2)).
Clause 1 of Bill C-22 would amend section 33 of CEPA by repealing subsection 33(2) of the Act and by making a consequential amendment to subsection 33(1) to accommodate the deletion of subsection 33(2). The effect of this amendment is to allow an order of the Governor in Council placing a substance on the List of Toxic Substances to take effect when it is made rather than when the regulations in respect of the substance are made. A considerable amount of time might pass between the making of an order and the coming into force of regulations during which the substance would technically not be on the List.
This amendment would ensure that the status List of Toxic Substances is not dependent on whether regulations are made under Section 34 of the Act. It is clear that subsection 33(2) is not essential to the statute's regulatory scheme and may in fact complicate the process of regulating toxic substances.
Section 34 of CEPA currently provides that where an order has been made adding a substance to the list of toxic substances in Schedule 1 of the Act the Governor in Council can, after an advisory committee has been given the opportunity to render its advice, make regulations in respect of the substance. It is important to note that this section states that regulations can be made only in respect of a substance that has been added to the List by an order of the Governor in Council.
There were a number of substances on the List of Toxic Substances when CEPA was passed. These substances are on the List not by virtue of an order in council but because they were already in the statute. Because Section 34 currently allows regulations to be made only in respect of substances that are on the List by an order of the Governor in Council, substances that became part of the List in any other manner cannot be regulated. It would appear, therefore, that there is no legislative basis under CEPA for regulating the substances contained on the List of Toxic Substances at the time the legislation was passed.
It should be noted that among the substances found on the List for which regulations cannot be made are chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), in respect of which the Canadian Government is committed to regulate under the 1987 Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer.
Clause 2 of Bill C-22 would remove from section 34 of CEPA the reference to orders placing a substance on the List of Toxic Substances, thereby making it clear that regulations can be made in respect of any substance found on the List.
We should look at exactly what is in Schedule 1 because this is what the nub of the amendment to Sections 33 and 34 is all about, albeit the Minister and the Government are particularly attuned to the July 1 date for the implementation of the 1987 Montreal Protocol. We find under Schedule I, which is the list of toxic substances passed by Parliament, the following
categories. There are chlorobiphenyls which have the molecular formula C12H10-nCln in which "n" is greater than 2. We have dodecachloropentacyclo decane. We have polybrominated biphenyls that have the molecular formula C12H10-nBm in which "n" is greater than 2. We have chlorofluorocarbon, totally halogenated chlorofluorocarbons that have the molecular formula CnClxF(2n-l-2-x). We have polychlorinated terphenyls that have a molecular formula C18H14-nCln in which "n" is greater than 2. There are four other families. I put those on the record to have some idea of how complicated the toxic substances in chemical families are. Then there are four that I think the Minister should have been here to address. There is asbestos, lead, mercury and vinyl chloride, substances that are extensively used and find their way into our environment.
Let us look at Bill C-22 because in fact it is going to require further amendments. I say that because when one looks at the wording of the new proposed Section 33 it says:
Subject to subsection (4), the Governor in Council may, if satisfied that a substance is toxic, on the recommendation of the Ministers, make an order adding the substance to the List of Toxic Substances in Schedule I.
I have just listed those before the House.
If one looks at the English version of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act as is statute law in Canada, what Section 33(1) says now is the following:
Subject to subsections (2) and (4), the Governor in Council may, if satisfied that a substance is toxic, on the recommendation of the Ministers, make an order adding the substance to the List of Toxic Substances in Schedule I.
So the amendment is quite clear in English. As one can see in C-22, the English amendment is listed both under the English section and under the French section.
This is where it becomes interesting and where all Members of this House should become increasingly suspicious of who is drafting this and why additional loopholes are being created without being forthright with Members of the House. You will have to excuse my pronunciation, Mr. Speaker, but I think you will understand the distinction between 33(1) as it is in English and in French in the Act now and what is being proposed in the English here will still no longer be comparable to the French that remains in the Act. The French in the Act says the following:
S'il est-qu'une substance est toxique, le gouvemeur en conseil peut prendre, sur recommandation des ministres, un decret d'inscription de la substance a la liste de VAnnexe I.

well as those Justice people who drafted the legislation, and officials from Environment Canada.
The Bill is only one page long. It is not an horrifically difficult Bill to deal with, but I certainly put the Government on notice that I want adequate explanations of why we are asked to amend a Bill in which there is such a distinct difference between the French and the English in the law.
I will return to CFCs themselves. I have not yet heard from the government side, and in particular the Minister, what serious steps he plans to take in relation to CFCs. He has been on notice for weeks through questions I have raised in the standing committee, questions raised by my friend from Davenport, and questions by others in relation to the problems with existing refrigeration units, whether those be refrigerators, freezers, air conditioners in cars, trucks, tractors, or heavy duty equipment in large buildings which is the place where most of the CFCs in Canada presently reside.
Many Canadians scratch their heads and wonder why, although the Government of Canada entertains these plans vis-a-vis CFCs and wants to be involved on July 1 in relation to the Montreal Protocol, we see the rolling loonie eveiy night on the television screen talking about Canada's sudden national debt of hundreds of millions of dollars. We ask ourselves why the steps are not being taken. We are asked to pass regulatory change which is basically functus. enforcement procedures. Are we to stop the dumping into land fill sites in the Quebec townships of refrigeration units coming from the United States? He did not choose this opportunity to come and speak on an issue of global importance and of great importance to Members of this House, particularly on this side.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It is a tradition of the House that we do not discuss the attendance or non-attendance of Members of Parliament in the House of Commons. The comments made by the Hon. Member at the end of his remarks, to which we listened to attentively, were totally uncalled for and I think he should apologize.

June 20, 1989
Environmental Protection

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Skeena is a long time Member and I am sure he knows that. I did not hear the remarks at the end of his speech, but if he made such remarks I am sure he will apologize.
Yes, I am very sorry that he is not here, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, this is a constructive debate, and I will continue in the same vein as my colleagues by drawing to the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary the fact that there may be another puzzling shortcoming in Bill C-22, namely, the omission from the French version of Bill C-22 the words "par decret", the equivalent of the term "by decree", which also is not present in the English version of the Bill.
Constitutional experts would draw to the attention of the Government the fact that such an omission would mean that the Standing Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments would not have the power to examine, in due course, the performance and the consistency of this Bill with other pieces of legislation.
Maybe the Parliamentary Secretary would like to make a note of it and check it with the overworked Department of Justice, which evidently reflects a low budget, too few lawyers for too much work, and the inability of the Government to provide enough resources in the Budget so that Bills are properly drafted.
I am sure that the Parliamentary Secretary understands and that he will look into this matter.
What worries us is that behind this measure is of course the urgent question of chlorofluorocarbons and how they might affect the ozone layer and human health. Others have already referred to it. I would like only to register through the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister the fact that while the Minister of the Environment has promised to reduce the production of chlorofluorocarbons by 85 per cent, the regulations that are being presently proposed would achieve only a reduction of 50 per cent. That would be a very disturbing, large gap.
I would hope, if that turns out not to be the case, that in his opening statement in committee the Minister will clarify this matter so that we will have a confirmation that the regulations are consistent with his promise. This
is very important because of the fact that the health of Canadians is at stake if we do not move quickly.
We also need to consider the necessity, if alternatives to chlorofluorocarbons are not technically in existence, to forgo certain products and to forgo certain uses, certain consumptions in society, because if we do not the damage is irrevocable. We are dealing here with the immune system of human beings, and therefore, with a very important and central question of health.
I would also reinforce the notion of others that the Bill would actually require further amendments. Unfortunately, this is not the case today, but we would certainly want to register with the Government the necessity to introduce further amendments. The law as it functions at the present time is flawed.
The Government at the present time cannot set enforceable national standards as demonstrated in the case of PCBs. I will go into that in a moment. Second, the Minister of the Environment is the only person in the country who can seek an injunction to stop a violation of the Act. Third, another shortcoming is that the law as it stands now lacks a general prohibition clause as we have in Section 33 of the Fisheries Act, which would make the release of any pollutant an offence, not just the ones listed in the schedules of the Act. This is a very central question. Finally, in the event of an emergency, the federal Government cannot move alone. Mandatory consultation with the provinces affected is required.
I will not elaborate at length on the lack of national enforceable standards. The enforceable national standards were lost between December 1986 when the proposed Environmental Protection Act was released as a draft for public discussion and the final clause by clause work in committee. Over the period between December 1986 and the spring of 1988, as a result of Meech Lake influence on the thinking of the Government, we lost the capacity for the federal Government to establish and impose enforceable national standards. I will not elaborate on how this took place. It makes very interesting reading.
All that needs to be said is that today we are asked, as a result of the law which was finally passed, to make a change in a law that at present indicates that no regulations could be made until after a federal-provincial advisory committee, and I quote, "is provided an opportunity to render its advice". That is how the Bill reads at the present time.
June 20, 1989

For some reason that phrase has to be amended through Bill C-22. The word "given" has to be substituted for the word "provided', and "provide" has to be substituted for the word "render". The new clause would now read that a federal-provincial advisory committee "is given an opportunity to provide its advice", instead of "is provided an opportunity to render its advice".
Since you probably understand, as a literary man, Mr. Speaker, the English language much better than I do, what is the difference between these two phrases? I have enormous difficulties in understanding it.
I followed very carefully the excellent presentation by the Parliamentary Secretary. He certainly gave us a very interesting technical insight into the reasons. However, when it comes to the language, which in the end what we have to look for, I really have difficulty understanding the difference between "is provided an opportunity to render its advice" and "is given an opportunity to provide its advice".
Maybe, when the Bill goes to committee, an explanation as to the profound semantic reasons for this change will be given so that we will be enlightened. We are in the dark. We do not know whether this amendment will strengthen the Bill from a federal point of view, whether this amendment will weaken it, or whether it will make it indifferent.
You will understand, Mr. Speaker, that as legislators some light needs to be cast. It is interesting to note that a former Minister of the Environment admitted that the weakening or the relinquishing of powers to the provinces in making national enforceable standards in the environment was a result of negotiations with the provinces behind closed doors. These negotiations were held at a time when the former committee was holding public hearings on the Bill preceding the one we are debating today. Of course we felt at that time as if a mockery was made of public consultations. When the various organizations appeared before us we were looking at a different Bill. It caused consternation and the quality of the relationships in committee was deeply affected.
Environmental Protection
We know what the result was when it came to PCBs in the aftermath of St. Basile le Grand. Safe storage was the first item on the agenda. The former Minister of the Environment was quoted as saying: "The actions I am taking ensure that PCB storage sites in every part of Canada meet high national standards".
Within two months nine provinces had sought from Ottawa to be exempted from such standards under the equivalency provisions of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
On May 12, 1989 all provinces except Prince Edward Island were granted exemption from high national standards. It must be noted and underlined that none of the provinces have the same penalties and fines in place which exist under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. Nor do the provinces guarantee the investigation of infractions of the law as the Canadian Environmental Protection does. Yet, it was ruled that provincial laws are equivalent.
In the case of PCBs-and I want to make this case to the Parliamentary Secretary who is patiently following this matter-instead of a single national standard for the storage of PCBs we have the federal national standard in P.E.I. and in the Territories. Then we have nine different provincial standards. We have uneven regulations which can lead to the creation of pollution havens where regulations are weakest. This unevenness is made worse by enforcement practices which vary from one province to another.
With PCBs we begin to see the emergence of a veritable environmental quilt. The environment is no longer a federal responsibility. It has been fragmented and Balkanized. Therefore, the experience with PCBs in the application of existing legislation erodes our confidence in the commitment of the Government to bring in tough enforceable national standards for the substances which have not yet been approached, such as CFCs, dioxins, furans, and other toxic substances. This is why we are preoccupied and why we must take the opportunity to raise this matter at second reading with the Government. The experience with PCBs is one that has led to a predictable Balkanization of standards. We urge the Government to ensure that the experience with PCBs does not repeat itself with other toxic substances which are included in the schedule the Parliamentary Secretary recited for us earlier in his presentation.

June 20, 1989
Environmental Protection

Mr. Speaker, I want to comment on some of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Davenport.
It is always a pleasure to listen to the Hon. Member for Davenport speak in this House about the environment. The Hon. Member comes by this honestly. As a matter of fact, people are just starting to get into some of the things that he has said about the environment. He was ahead of his time. I want to say that to him, and I wish he were the environment critic for the Liberal Party. I say to him not to worry. He will resurface because he has the knowledge and vision about the environment, together of course with my own colleague, the Hon. Member for Skeena who also has the environment in his bones. There are some comments I did not understand. If the Parliamentary Secretary wants to talk about acid rain back to 1979, that is fine.
What the Hon. Member for Davenport underlined about this Bill is very important. This is a Bill to amend the Environmental Protection Act which was a law enacted last year. I had the pleasure-sometimes it wasn't too pleasurable; it was a lot of work-to sit for a couple of weeks on the legislative committee that considered the Bill. The committee went through the Bill clause by clause. The Hon. Member for Davenport said where we failed in that Bill was to establish enforceable national standards. The Government originally had that as a concept. The former Minister of the Environment, Mr. McMillan, had that in the Bill. Then he ran into the opposition of the provincial environmental Ministers, and he withdrew this national thrust from the Bill. The committee members asked the Minister what would happen if there were a spill of PCBs or another disaster. Subsequently we have seen a spill of PCBs on the Trans-Canada Highway, a fire in St. Basile le Grand, oil spills on the coast, and other things. The environment became a national crisis, and Canadian people by any standard consider it the number one issue.
The Hon. Member for Davenport pointed out quite rightly that this Bill lacks enforceable national standards. What the Government should be doing is bringing in amendments to put these standards in the Bill.
Finally is the concept of the public being able to sue polluters of the environment; not just the Ministry of the Environment, which may do nothing but do as California does and give the public rights to take polluters to court. Where there is a polluting chemical company such as in Port Moody, the local residents would have authority under a federal Act with a national enforceable standard to go to court against that company. Then we would see some real action on the environment. I would like the Hon. Member to comment on these matters, but he need not comment on the nice things I said about him.

Mr. Speaker, it is impossible to disagree at this stage. Therefore, I am glad that the Hon. Member sees the necessity as we do of having national enforceable standards. He has developed the issue extremely well and I am very grateful to him.
Anyone who believes in strong federalism and does not think the answer to Canada's problem is the devolution of power to the provinces feels very strongly that beginning with the environment, followed by spending powers, by aboriginal rights, and a number of other crucial issues is one, we must stay on the road of strong federal powers.
The Canadian Environmental Protection Act is a classic example of where a Minister of the Crown, having first introduced a Bill which did have the measure required to establish national enforceable standards in the environment, had then to turn 180 degrees and abandon that track. We regret it very much. If everyone in this House feels as strongly about the environment as does the Hon. Member who just spoke, I am sure that we can amend the Bill at a future opportunity to have enforceable national standards in the federal legislation.

subsubtopic: CMHC FUNDING FOR PRINCE CHARLES SENIORS PROJECT

Mr. Speaker, "Protect children on the farm" is the theme for National Farm Safety Week, July 25 to 31, organized by the Canada Safety Council with Agriculture Canada and in cooperation with provincial safety organizations and the Farm Safety Association.

June 20, 1989
Growing up on a farm can be a wonderful experience for children, but by its nature, a farm is a dangerous place and every year, many children lose their life or are injured in accidents there.
Mr. Speaker, children are our future. Let us protect them! This year, fanners will be made aware of their responsibility for their children's safety, which involves identifying and eliminating accident risks, setting a good example and informing young people about the safety rules to observe in buildings and around livestock and machines, both indoors and outdoors.

subsubtopic: TWINNING OF WHITBY, ONTARIO AND LONGUEUIL, QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we approach Canada Day, a time for all citizens to celebrate their citizenship, we should all use the opportunity to take stock of our many blessings as a nation where peace and prosperity abound.
Twenty-two years ago, a company of venturers from the Boy Scout movement of Whitby, Ontario, reversed the route taken by Jacques Cartier and arrived in Longueuil, Quebec. This trip culminated in some dialogue, and the decision to have a twinning program between the two communities.
The citizens of each municipality, with the active support of their local municipal councils, have for 21 years now sent delegations to visit each other to learn and promote a better understanding of their cultures and communities. For three days each year, 50 residents of each community are hosted in an excellent setting of friendship and goodwill.
The reason I bring this to your attention, Mr. Speaker, is so that you and other Members of the House can take this idea back to your own ridings and encourage your citizens to undertake a similar program. Would it not be great if we could influence more Canadian municipalities to twin with other municipalities and follow the lead of Whitby, Ontario, and Longueuil, Quebec.
Congratulations to both municipalities for doing their part in making Canada such a great place to live.

subsubtopic: SITUATION OF THE TURKISH MOSLEM IN BULGARIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last few days, we have received many reports that thousands of Bulgarian citizens belonging to the Turkish Moslem minority were issued passports and suddenly expelled to neighboring countries. Press reports indicate that the number might be over 30,000. This sudden exodus is of great concern to Canadians. Since 1984, they have been very concerned by the Bulgarian authorities' assimilation campaign which has resulted in name changes and restrictions on the use of the Tbrkish language and expressions of Tbrkish culture.
On Friday, June 16, at the Paris conference, Canada's Ambassador, William Bauer, strongly criticized the treatment given to the Turkish Moslem minority in Bulgaria and in particular, the recent expulsions. He drew attention to the human suffering caused by the Bulgarian authorities.
I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) remains concerned by a situation that raises tensions in the Balkans and detracts from cooperation and security in Europe. I am pleased to point out that on Friday, June 16, he issued a communique expressing Canada's concern about the recent expulsions and the Bulgarian charge d'affaires was called in so that our disapproval of his government's actions could be conveyed to him.

Mr. Speaker, a proposed business plan of VIA Rail recently obtained by The Globe and Mail has confirmed some of the worst fears held by Atlantic Canadians. The proposed cutbacks have guaranteed a minimum of 2,500 employee lay-offs, as well as the complete elimination of all regional train services. This is in light of the election promise to enhance the quality and reliability of VIA services.
June 20, 1989

I find it disturbing that various cabinet Ministers have praised the new Budget for helping the welfare of the Atlantic provinces. In reality, Atlantic Canada is being ruined by the incredible burden it has to assume in dealing with the current deficit. Major cuts in ERDAs, ACOA, VIA Rail, and the closing of Canadian Forces bases have promised to inflict devastating impacts upon the region.
I call upon the Government to reassess the negative priorities applied to Atlantic Canada. This region, which recently began upon the road of economic recovery, has once again been thrown into a situation that guarantees hard times in the Maritimes. Atlantic Canadians should be allowed to reap the benefits of economic success.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday more than 300 Islanders travelled to Ottawa to make it clear to the Government how they feel about the closing of Canadian Forces Base Summerside. Yet the Government has not made it clear to the people of Prince Edward Island what research was carried out to back up this reckless decision.
What is frightening is that this decision, which will seriously affect the economy of Summerside and the entire province, was made without an impact study. The people of Prince Edward Island deserve better.
I demand that the Government take responsibility for its actions against Summerside and area and keep the base open.
In all fairness, the federal Government cannot arbitrarily decide to shut down one-third of a community's workforce. Islanders have proved that they are determined and ready to keep CFB Summerside open, and my colleagues and I are determined to support them.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to answer a question posed by the Premier of Nova Scotia last night after a starry-eyed meeting with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) regarding cuts in development funds that have devastated Atlantic Canada when he stated: "Cuts? What cuts?" I am here today to edify the Premier of Nova Scotia and answer those questions for him.
First, I would like to remind the Premier of Nova Scotia that in Nova Scotia alone there are six subagreements that have not been renewed; $721 million in cuts in Atlantic Canada alone. That, Mr. Premier, is a cut. Second, he should check the books and Hansard and he will find out that the ACOA program in Atlantic Canada has been extended from five years to seven years. It does not take a mathematical genius to know that that is a 25 per cent cut, Mr. Premier, in the money that is available in Atlantic Canada.
What about VIA Rail and the cuts that have been inflicted by this Government in Atlantic Canada? There is also the closure of the route from Truro to Sydney. In the Halifax area alone the reduction of service could cost 321 jobs. That, Mr. Premier, is a cut. The At and East program, as stripped down in the last federal Budget, could see 297 individuals who work at the grain terminal in Halifax lose their jobs. Mr. Premier, that is a cut.
Does the Premier not know a cut when he sees a cut? Perhaps before he gets up the next time and sticks his proverbial foot in his proverbial mouth he can give me a call at (613) 995-9378 and I will straighten him out.

Mr. Speaker, from June 18 to June 21 the federal Government will be hosting a national forum on the prevention of family violence.
Family violence is a serious and widespread problem affecting the lives of countless Canadians. An estimated one in ten women and tens of thousands of children and elderly people are the victims of violence. The scars, both physical and emotional, can last a lifetime. The forum is being held as part of the federal Government's initiative to deal with this serious problem.
"Working Together" is the title given to the forum. It brings together about 400 individuals from all across Canada who are involved in the prevention of family violence. They represent health and social service agencies, voluntary and non-government organizations, provincial and territorial Governments, women's groups and community groups, native organizations, the business community and the legal community.
It is only by working together toward a national strategy to reduce family violence that we can expect to find long-term solutions.
I would like to wish the participants a busy and productive three days.
June 20, 1989

subsubtopic: THE PASSING OF THE MAYOR OF BEAUPRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the town of Beaupre was in mourning during the weekend, following the death of Mr. Antoine Belanger, for nearly 20 years the mayor of this sizable municipality in the riding of Montmorency-Orleans.
As mayor, Mr. Belanger was very much involved in the development of Mont Sainte-Anne, now an internationally known ski centre.
At the federal level, Mr. Belanger sat in the House of Commons from 1962 to 1969 as the Social Credit Member for Charlevoix, which then included the town of Beaupre.
With all the people of Beaupre and the former riding of Charlevoix, I wish to pay tribute to this man of action and extend my sincere condolences to his family and friends.

Mr. Speaker, on June 20, 1981, half a million people were gathered together in the city of Tehran to take part in a peaceful demonstration in opposition to the suppression of democratic rights in Iran.
In response to this protest, the Iranian regime led by the Ayatollah Khomeini, ordered guards to open fire on the marchers. Hundreds were killed or wounded. Those who escaped the gunfire were arrested and transported to the Evin Prison where the firing squads continued into 1988 with their mass executions. To date, the number of those executed without just trial is reported to have reached over 90,000.
On the eighth anniversary of this bloody massacre I urge the Government of Canada to communicate to the new regime of Iran its horror at the flagrant human rights violations that have now been going on steadily for eight years, and its intention that if this trend continues Canada will seriously reconsider its trade and diplomatic relations with that country.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I noted with interest in the newspapers today that July 3 is tax freedom day, the day on which Canadians finally start working for themselves.
Tax freedom day has been moving back further each year as taxes increase. The middle-class of Canada feels quite burdened by the taxes that they have to pay now. At the moment the middle-class is tired of paying an excessive amount of tax for debt servicing.
Thank goodness that Canadians can look forward to an equal, equitable and fair tax system which is contemplated for the future.
Thank goodness there is one rate, fair for all with no exceptions.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
For two years, the Minister has been telling us, and I quote: "Sales tax reform will eliminate the hidden taxes paid by consumers when they purchase goods." That is what we have been hearing for two years, and it just isnt't true! The Minister was forced to admit today that the new national sales tax will not appear on the bills for the billions and billions of dollars worth of items to which the new federal sales tax will apply.

I want to refer the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to page 25 of the booklet entitled The Goods and Services Tax. It states:
-the government will want the advice of consumer groups on:
how best to ensure that consumers know the amount of tax they are
paying on their purchases while, at the same time, maintaining the
simplicity of the tax system;

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, the Consumers Association of Canada said today that the Minister's response is not good enough, that consumers have a right to know the amount of tax they are paying.
I did not think the credibility of the Minister of Finance could sink any lower. He says that he will replace one hidden tax with another hidden tax. For two years he swore in the House and across the country that the new federal sales tax would not be a hidden tax. Now he claims to journalists, apparently, that he has no constitutional power to force retailers to add the sales tax to the sales slip. That is absolute nonsense.
If he had such a legal opinion, why did he not say so two years ago, or is he claiming that officials hid that legal opinion from him for two years? If he did know, did he just choose not to say so during the election campaign?
Is it not the real truth that the Minister is now desperately trying to find a way to justify a hidden tax?

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition is correct. The Government of Canada does not have the constitutional right to impose its will on retailers as to whether or not it will be tax included pricing or tax excluded pricing.
We have said very clearly that this tax will be much clearer to people than the tax on manufactured products which is buried right at the manufactured level, not at the wholesale or retail level. It is right down at the manufactured level. This tax will be quite clear at the retail level.
I should point out to the Leader of the Opposition that if we had a national sales tax, then the provinces would have been part of that and we would have made our views very clear at that time.

Mr. Speaker, let us be clear. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. Since the signing of the Free Trade Agreement we have seen a consistent procession of Canadian industries moving their jobs into the United States sun belt or into the Maquiladora zone of Mexico. The latest example is the 400 high skilled jobs of Bendix Corporation in Collingwood moving to Alabama and into the Maquiladora region.
Considering that his own officials consistently have refused to take any actions to plug those loopholes by which Canadian industry can evade the content requirements and can seek out areas of cheap labour, what will the Government do to stop this leakage of Canadian employment into those areas, denying Canadians the right to work and denying Canadian industry the right to grow? Does the Government have any plan to deal with this clearly serious problem for this economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT CLOSURE OF BENDIX CORP.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has been trade critic long enough to know that what he is presenting to the House now is completely spurious and false.
This loss of jobs at Bendix in Collingwood, Ontario is most regrettable but it has nothing to do with the Free Trade Agreement.
Oral Questions

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT CLOSURE OF BENDIX CORP.
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT CLOSURE OF BENDIX CORP.
speechtext: It has nothing to do with the Free Trade Agreement. The business produces auto parts and it has been under the Auto Pact for 24 years, since the Auto Pact came into being in Canada. Under the Auto Pact there is free trade in original equipment, automotive parts, between Canada and the United States. The company would have been free to make this decision at any time in the last 24 years or anytime in the next 24 years, but it is not permitted or given any grounds for making the decision, nor is it assisted in coming to such a decision by the U.S-Canada Free Trade Agreement. It is a matter of the Auto Pact. The hon. gentleman knows that. He is dishonest in attempting to suggest that this is a result of the U.S-Canada Free Trade Agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT CLOSURE OF BENDIX CORP.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been trade critic long enough to know that any answer from that Minister is totally spurious. It is unfortunate that a Trade Minister of the Government is not aware that under the Free Trade Agreement the content requirements under the Auto Pact were changed, requiring North American content, not Canadian content. That is what makes a difference.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada itself refuses to undertake any monitoring of this major leakage of Canadian jobs. The Canadian Government, in discussions we had today with U.S. customs officials, has refused or has been negligent in requesting U.S. customs to take any monitoring or inspection of those matters. When will the Government take serious action to deal with the serious problems resulting in a serious loss of jobs for this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TFade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we know what the theory of the Official Opposition is, because it was given to us by their finance critic: "Every sparrow that falls will be blamed on the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement". He said: "The trade deal will be blamed even if it may or may not be to blame". There is the photograph of the person. He is sitting just down the aisle from the you, Mr. Speaker. The Free Trade Agreement had nothing to do with this situation, but we are monitoring what is happening.

June 20, 1989
Oral Questions
For every incident that the hon. gentleman can cite, I have two or three which show that because of the Free Trade Agreement more plants and manufacturing companies are expanding in Canada. For example, Dupont Canada purchased a site in Trenton to manufacture food containers for frozen meals, and the reason given was the Free Trade Agreement. The same is true in Windsor, Scarborough, Mississauga, Smiths Falls, Montreal-
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: THE NEW SALES TAX-ELECTORAL PROMISES-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Here is a Minister who cannot keep the promises he made regarding his new sales tax.
First of all, he promised the tax would be revenue neutral, which it will not be. And second, according to the Minister the tax would eliminate existing hidden taxes, which is not going to happen. Third, we are now witnessing the violation of his third promise: the new tax itself will be hidden.
Could the Minister explain why he has once again broken a promise he made to Canadians?

subsubtopic: THE NEW SALES TAX-ELECTORAL PROMISES-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, no promises have been broken here. I just want to remind the Hon. Member that before she gets too far out on a limb she should reflect back on the tax probe of her Party which said: "Our analysis has led us to conclude that the current federal sales tax is so unfair, unaccountable and administratively complex that it should be abolished".

subsubtopic: THE NEW SALES TAX-ELECTORAL PROMISES-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: THE NEW SALES TAX-ELECTORAL PROMISES-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Perhaps the Hon. Member has some way of bringing in a sales tax that can achieve that. Obviously her Party says that it should be abolished.
I have responded to the Leader of the Opposition on the same sort of question, but let me say to her that the new tax will be at the same rate at the retail level on all taxable items across the board. Therefore it will be much, much easier for consumers to know how much tax they will be paying, even if the tax is included in the price.
We are not saying today that it will be included or excluded. What I said to the Leader of the Opposition was that we do not have the power to enforce that, but we will be working with the Consumers' Association of Canada and other organizations to find the best way of achieving that very important element of visibility for the consumer.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister severely criticized the existing sales tax system. I would remind him that the existing hidden sales and excise tax costs every man, woman, and child in Canada $268 a year at this time. The Minister said in 1987:
Many Canadians are unaware of this tax because it is normally applied when a produce is manufactured and is hidden in the price of goods- By the time it reaches the consumer, a dollar of tax paid by a manufacturer can raise the price to the consumer by a lot more than a dollar, and the purchaser does not know much.
I would like to ask the Minister to tell the House how the new sales tax is going to differ from the old sales tax.

Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted to do just that because the Hon. Member is absolutely right.
I have roundly criticized the existing tax as has her Party, as has the Liberal Party. It is a bad tax. The reason why it is a bad tax is that the existing tax is buried deep in the production of the particular product. When it reaches the retail level, the tax may be 3 per cent, it may be 5 per cent, it may be 10 per cent, or it may be 13.5 per cent. Surely that is an unfair tax.
What will happen with this tax is that it will be 9 per cent on all taxable goods at the retail level. That makes it much fairer. That makes it much clearer to the consumer. That is one of the key reasons why we are supportive of this tax. It is one of the key reasons why I believe her Party should also be supportive of this tax.
June 20, 1989
Canadians cannot be that easily fooled. They know that a hidden tax is a tax that can be raised without them seeing where it is going to.

Mr. Speaker, a new 9 per cent tax is supposed to mean a break for consumers on the price of manufactured goods such as cars, household furniture, and appliances which are currently taxed at 13.5 per cent after the recent Budget.
If this tax remains hidden, how can Canadians be sure that they are getting this break that he says we are going to get in the new sales tax?
Mr. Speaker, we will be making that quite clear when the technical paper is released.
Oh, oh!

Let me remind the Hon. Member of another reason why her Party should be fully in support of this tax. The New Democratic Party says that loopholes for the rich are bad. One clear element of this sales tax is that there are no loopholes.
Any time persons purchases a product that is taxable, they pay that tax. The rich cannot tax plan themselves out of this. They cannot hire lawyers or accountants or anybody like that to tax plan them out of paying that tax. It is payable by everyone. Furthermore, there is an offset to low income Canadians which ensures that this tax is a fair tax for low income Canadians.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF CFB SUMMERSIDE-IMPACT ON SEARCH AND RESCUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the House yesterday the Minister of National Defence stated in his response to my question on the search and rescue component now at CFB Summerside that search and rescue was identified on budget day and that that was still the policy and direction they were prepared to take.
Will the Minister confirm, more specifically, that search and rescue will not only remain in Prince Edward Island as stated on budget day, but that it will remain in Summerside since it will cost many millions of dollars to have it placed elsewhere?
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF CFB SUMMERSIDE-IMPACT ON SEARCH AND RESCUE

Member is aware that the necessity to close CFB Summerside was to bring about a savings to this Government because of the lack of operational need of that base. Mr. Speaker, if I recall correctly, what the budget statement said was that it would be located in Prince Edward Island, that it would be located in Charlottetown.
The Minister said that he was saving money by moving the search and rescue to Charlottetown and that it would cost many millions.
