subsubtopic: IMPACT OF FREE TRADE AGREEMENT ON ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Egmont of course is dead right when he says that the Government ought to be increasing not decreasing surveillance, particularly over fishing.
I have a question for my good friend, the Minister of Fisheries, about the overfishing which is devastating the Atlantic economy. Yesterday we learned that Fishery Products International, FPI, suffered a $7 million loss in the first quarter, that it is buying fish from South America and Alaska, and then processing it in the United States.

June 20, 1989
Oral Questions
Is FPI's policy of purchasing fish in other countries and processing it in the United States just the latest example of what free trade is going to mean to Atlantic Canada-creating jobs in the United States instead of here in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subsubtopic: IMPACT OF FREE TRADE AGREEMENT ON ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has made certain allegations. I am unaware of the factual basis on which those allegations are made. I would certainly want to look into that question before I would accept any assertion made by the Hon. Member opposite on such a question.
I also note that the president of Fishery Products International only yesterday was quoted as saying that he was very optimistic about the outlook for Fishery Products International in terms of returning to a profitable position by, I think, the third quarter of this year.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF FREE TRADE AGREEMENT ON ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext: What allegations? That there is overfishing? Does the Minister not know that there is overfishing? Does he not know that FPI has lost a bundle this year and that it is buying fish abroad?

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the same Minister. The crisis in the Atlantic Fishery is having a devastating vicious chain reaction. Fishing incomes are down or wiped out. Shipyards are laying off people. The construction industry is in a tailspin. I could go on.
Is it necessary for the people of Atlantic Canada to beg this Government for help? Where is the plan the Minister promised this House three full weeks ago, the plan to help those people caught in the middle of the Government's mismanagement and kowtowing to the foreigners.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I made the observation last week, but I will make it again today. The Hon. Member should apologize to the people of his area and of Atlantic Canada for spreading totally unjustified alarm and fear. The inshore fishery of his own region is only beginning to get under way for the 1989 fishing year.
Under the last four successive years of fisheries management by the Government, employment in the Atlantic fishery and income have continued to increase to unprecedented levels.

subtopic: PRESENCE OF NICK PRICE AT CANADIAN OPEN GOLF TOURNAMENT
PRESENCE OF NICK PRICE AT CANADIAN OPEN GOLF TOURNAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport.
The Canadian Open Golf Tournament takes place this weekend. The Minister will be aware that South African golfer Nick Price, travelling on a British passport of convenience, is attending the tournament. The Minister will also be aware that this is in complete contradiction of the policy the Canadian Government announced last year.
Will the Government enforce its own policy and prohibit Nick Price from entering Canada to participate in the tournament? Will it call on the Royal Canadian Golf Association to withdraw its invitation to Mr. Price?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PRESENCE OF NICK PRICE AT CANADIAN OPEN GOLF TOURNAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's policy in the area of sport contact with South Africa is derived from the 1977 Gleneagles Agreement. As the Member has mentioned, there has been a review of that policy as applied in Canada less than a year ago and a tightening up of the policy. Since then there has been a further review of how the policy now applies in Canada to consider further ways in which we can tighten it up.
Mr. Price is coming into Canada under a passport from the U.K. I am sorry to say that in those circumstances Canada is not in a position in which we can question the legal documents that have been put out by the Government of the U.K.
However, I will add that I will intervene personally with the Royal Canadian Golf Association and invite it to decline from inviting Mr. Price to play in its golf tournament.
June 20,1989

subtopic: PRESENCE OF NICK PRICE AT CANADIAN OPEN GOLF TOURNAMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope the Government is not too late. It has had notice of this situation for some time.

Mr. Speaker, is the Minister also aware that seven golfers, including yesterday's U.S. Open Champion Curtis Strange, Lee Trevino, Ben Crenshaw, Ken Green, and Nick Faldo, who have thumbed their noses at the UN boycott of sports contacts with South Africa and who, as a result, are on the UN register for sports contact with South Africa, intend to participate in the Open?
Will the Government enforce the UN black list and will it act to preserve the threat against the Commonwealth Games in Auckland and Victoria and in order to preserve Canada's reputation on the issue of apartheid?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you will know, this is a very important issue for the Government of Canada and that is why there was a tightening up of the policy less than a year ago. One of the things we did at that time was to deny visa to those athletes, whether professional or amateur, attempting to enter Canada for sporting events. Even though there was that tightening up, we are looking at ways now in which we can do more things.
The difficulty we have in the very specific situation of a professional event is that they come under legal documents put forward by other countries. That obviously sets a limit on our level of action, but we will be speaking with those sport associations which have this type of activity to encourage them not to invite these athletes and to maintain Canada's position of having one of the strongest policies against sporting contacts with South Africa.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO CHINESE NATIONALS IN CANADA
speechtext:

Oral Questions
As Members will know, some thousands of Chinese citizens, many of them students, have found themselves caught in a most difficult situation here in Canada. They are quite concerned about what their future situation will be with respect to staying on in Canada.
Does the Minister intend to take further steps to assist these people? If so, can she indicate to the House what those measures might be?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO CHINESE NATIONALS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have said in the House before, we are constantly looking at our policy with regard to Chinese Nationals in Canada. There are two important things that I would like to clarify today. One of them is a new step which we are prepared to take.

Public information sessions have been held at various locations, and I would encourage people with questions to get in touch with them.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RATE IN CERTAIN MONTREAL NEIGHBOURHOODS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Today, Montreal's commission for economic development published a report indicating that the unemployment rate in 23 neighbourhoods in Montreal is over 15 per cent, while in 6 it is over 20 per cent. For instance, in Park Extension, the rate is 21 per cent, which is more than Sept-Iles with the same population, and in Plateau Mont Royal, it is 18 per cent, which is more than Abitibi with the same population.

June 20, 1989
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, considering these circumstances, when will this Government be ready to implement a special economic program for Montreal, in order to create jobs and reduce poverty? When?

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RATE IN CERTAIN MONTREAL NEIGHBOURHOODS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course, since September 1984, 315,000 jobs have been created in Quebec, and many of these in Montreal. Since we came to power, the unemployment rate has dropped from 13 per cent to 9.8 per cent, a decline of 3.2 per cent. The other day, the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Bourassa, mentioned that the economy of Montreal was in better shape now that it had been in decades, and I think he is right. There is investment. Things are happening in Montreal. The boom is strong and sustained, largely thanks to investment brought about by the unusual degree of co-operation between the federal Government and the Government of Quebec, which has generated a considerable number of jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest the Prime Minister read the report that was published in Montreal this morning.
The report says that the situation is worse now than it was in the recession of 1981 with over 400,000 unemployed in 23 Montreal districts. This was confirmed by the January report Deux Quebec dans un and the recent report of the Canadian Council on Social Development.
On June 7 the Minister of Labour, who is responsible for the City of Montreal, said that the Government had no special programs in mind for the City of Montreal. In view of the report tabled today in Montreal, would the Government now reconsider that approach and take steps with the City of Montreal and the Government of Quebec to reverse this deplorable situation in that city?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend mentions the year 1981 involving his Government. During the term of the last Liberal Government, in almost five years, 55 months, there were
40.000	jobs created in Quebec. In four years there were
315.000	jobs created in the Province of Quebec under the Progressive Conservative Government.

That is a big difference, 315,000.
My hon. friend points out that there are areas of economic difficulty in some areas of Montreal. I agree with him. We are trying to work very closely with the Province of Quebec, the City of Montreal, and the private sector to try to alleviate difficulties in those various sectors. However, generally speaking there has been a remarkable improvement in the economy of the Province of Quebec and in the growth of the City of Montreal. My hon. friend is a Montrealer; he is fully acquainted with that.
Under this Government jobs have been created in the Province of Quebec at a rate eight times faster than jobs were created under the previous Liberal Government. My hon. friend should be celebrating that tremendous contribution to Quebec's economic well-being rather than being a doomster and a gloomster like he has been all his life.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF RRAP FOR RENTAL HOUSING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Housing. Yesterday in Montreal, the provincial minister, the mayors of Montreal and Quebec City, the president of the provincial municipalities' union and others denounced the abolition of RRAP for rental housing as an act of blatant discrimination against Quebec. My question is: Was the Minister aware that by cutting this program, he was hitting the poorest in the Province of Quebec hardest, because they received 50 per cent of the funds under this program? If the answer is yes, why did he single them out, and if the answer is no, is he prepared to revive the RRAP for rental housing immediately and without delay?

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF RRAP FOR RENTAL HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sympathize with Quebec's problem. The RRAP for rental housing was used more in Quebec than elsewhere in Canada because 65 per cent of Quebecers are tenants. In the rest of Canada, only 38 per cent of the population rent their housing.
Yesterday, I told this House that I hope to form a tripartite federal-provincial-municipal committee which will find a solution to this problem. The question was raised yesterday by the Hon. Member for Chicoutimi. Unfortunately, the Hon. Member was not here at that time.

subsubtopic: ABOLITION OF RRAP FOR RENTAL HOUSING
speechtext:
Read the report.
June 20, 1989

Mr. Speaker, by cutting the program, the Government not only cut an essential program; it cut it without consultation with the provincial Governments concerned. The tripartite idea flown here yesterday has not impressed the provincial minister of housing, nor the mayor. The provincial minister said yesterday that he was going to take the Government to court. He said that the Government broke a federal-provincial agreement.
The total absence of consultation is breaking federal-provincial agreements. It is breaking the Government's word. Is that the way the Government intends to pursue the housing crisis in this country?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is aware of the difficulties we have with the fiscal situation in this country. When a program is not funded unfortunately there is no money to carry it out.
I regret that and I know that all members of the Government regret that fact. I am looking forward to working with the Hon. Member and all the Hon. Members in the House from Quebec and across the country to find some solutions to that problem.

Mr. Speaker, over 26,000 jobs have been lost by Canadian workers, men and women, to the United States and Mexico since the free trade deal has been instituted.
In answer to the question the Minister was asked about another 400 jobs being lost in Mexico, the Minister attacked the Liberal Party.
Does he have something to offer concretely in the terms that the Prime Minister said, that we would have the best programs of readjustment on the Free Trade Agreement of anywhere in the world? What does he specifically have to offer the 26,000 people who have already lost their jobs? Another 400 jobs are going to Mexico because of your bungling of the Free Trade Agreement?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has not come up with a sparrow. He has come with an albatross-
You are the albatross.

-and it is hanging around his neck. There are no such 26,000 jobs. There have been 1.4 million jobs created since the Government came into office. From time to time I am able to give other examples of jobs which have been created as a result of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
There is Alcan Aluminium, a $48 million modernization and expansion in Kitimat. That is in British Columbia. There is Cargill, a $50 million slaughterhouse in High River which will employ 480 by mid-summer 1989. That is a slaughterhouse. There is Novacor Chemicals of Calgary, $600 million in an ethylene plant near Joffre, creating 200 permanent jobs. There are no 26,000 jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I have in my hands a document which comes from the Commissioner of Customs in the United States. It indicates that goods brought into the United States from the Maquiladora section of Mexico will be treated under many circumstances as having U.S. origin.
What is this Government going to do to plug this loophole and to safeguard thousands of jobs right across this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had sparrows and we have had albatrosses. Now we have a canard or several canards.
There are clear provisions in the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. You have to show, in order to get the benefits of the agreement, that the goods originated in the United States or in Canada.
I do not know what obscure little document the hon. gentleman has from the U.S. Customs. However, their documents do not matter to us. It is our documents which matter to us. Our Customs will not allow such goods to come across the border subject to the U.S.-Canada tariff arrangements unless they show the goods originated in the United States, not in the Maquiladora, not in Mexico, and not in anywhere south of the border.

June 20, 1989
Oral Questions THE BUDGET

Mr. Speaker, as part of its promise to the Canadian voters that culture would not be on the free trade table, the Government undertook that postal subsidies would be maintained for at least five years.
In spite of that promise, the Budget Papers state that the postal subsidy will be cut by $10 million in 1989-90 and $45 million in each subsequent year. At this pace the program will be totally wiped out before the next election.
My question is for the Minister of Finance. While we know where the first $10 million is going to go that the Government is going to cut, we want to know what will be affected by the next $45 million? Over how many years is it going to take place? Where will the Minister stop, when the total $164 million infrastructure program is completely gone?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is well aware that this infrastructure program has been in place for a long period of time. It has not had much by way of review over the last many years.
What we are doing as a part of the budget process is reviewing all aspects of this program. The Hon. Member knows that there are publications which should not be getting this subsidy. It is those publications which will be identified, and they will cease to get the subsidy.
The Minister of Communications, working with the Minister responsible for the Post Office, will be coming up with proposals in that regard.
It is very clear where the $45 million cut is going to stop.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same Minister.
Could the Minister tell us why the Government has chosen not to support cultural magazines, ethnic magazines and not to support third language newspapers, community newspapers and daily newspapers when the Department of Communications study has shown that these subjects, supplementaries, and subsidies are absolutely fundamental to the survival of these particular magazines and newspaper?
It is important to small town Canada and rural Canada. Why is this Government not giving fair access to all Canadians across Canada?
Mr. Speaker, this normally is not the style of the Hon. Member to distort what we are trying to achieve with a program.
No. I am telling you the reality.
What we have said is that it is about time governments reviewed all forms of subsidy. This is one of those which we think it is important we should be reviewing.
The Italians, the Hungarians, the Greeks-everybody will be happy!

The Minister of Communications will be coming forward with proposals in this regard but clearly the Hon. Member is falling into the same trap of not wanting to review where moneys are spent. Keep the deficit running up. Keep the debt of the country running up. Forget about the impact that this has on interest rates, the impact of those interest rates on the very people about which she is concerned. This is what we are doing as a government and we feel it is the responsible approach to take.
My colleague will be bringing forward proposals which will demonstrate clearly that we are sensitive to a number of the concerns that she has raised.

subsubtopic: CONSTITUTIONAL POWER TO TAX-LEGAL OPINION QUESTIONED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two short questions for the Minister of Finance. Is he aware that the federal Government under our Constitution has the power to tax from all sources? Having that power he has the power fully to administer the tax including the power to describe the amount of the tax on any good affected by the tax. If he has a contrary legal opinion, would he table it in the House of Commons?
June 20,1989

Leader is fully aware-and he has a little smirk on his face, Mr. Speaker-that this is something not within the domain of the federal Government.

subsubtopic: CONSTITUTIONAL POWER TO TAX-LEGAL OPINION QUESTIONED

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance had this position documented by legal officers of the Crown, why did he not reveal the position two years ago instead of promising Canadians for the last two years that the new national sales tax would not be a hidden tax?

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by commenting on the main theme point in the Speech from the Throne in which the Government told us that the environment and its preservation for future generations were the Government's top priority.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. Members who wish to carry on a conversation will please converse behind the curtains.

I noticed that by the time the Throne Speech had faded a bit and we were into the Budget, suddenly the title of the Budget was not sustainable economic growth but sustained economic growth with no reference to sustainable.
That brings me to some of the points that I am concerned about with regard to this Bill. I do not believe any of us dispute the purpose of the Bill. I do think we have some concerns, however, about the commitment to the intention of the Bill and to the actions that are needed to go along with it. The reason we are being asked today to approve this Bill, and with minimum debate because of its urgency, is to allow the Government to implement its stated intentions to reduce the production of CFCs and their release into the environment.
We have no question in our minds that the environment, in particular the atmosphere, is the main issue that confronts society in Canada and around the world today. It is quite simply a question of whether there will be anything left to breathe a few years from now. If there is not, there will be no life on earth. For that reason, we have to question some of the weaknesses in the Bill. We have to question the lack of national standards that can be implemented. We have to question why, if this is such an important issue, the enforceability of this Bill is weak. We have to question why we are doing the minimum in targets for the reduction of CFCs being released into the atmosphere.
By contrast, I look at the actions of the Ontario Government which has introduced a package to eliminate the use of CFCs in Ontario completely. I note that part and parcel of Ontario's announcement was a commitment to commission and to fund the research and development necessary for a safe and efficient destruction method for CFCs.

June 20, 1989
Environmental Protection
We have heard and we will continue to hear in this House, at least from this side of the House, about the lack of commitment to science, research and technology development in this country. That is particularly important in the case of the CFC legislation and in the case of all environmental programs. This type of control, when it is only there as a mandatory kind of thing and not as part of a total commitment to the soundness of the environment, to improving it for future generations and certainly not to damaging it, is tokenism at best.
I am concerned that this Bill does not mean an awful lot. Over the last few years there have been reductions in research and development in energy conservation and the development of energy alternatives. There has been a reduction by 75 per cent of control of fertilizers and a lack of commitment to add resources to control the approval of pesticides and, in fact, to go back and review pesticides that have been approved and are now in use, based on our current knowledge of the environment and of the damage that pesticides can do both to the environment and to humanity.
I anticipate the same problem with CFCs: no commitment to research and development for alternatives, no commitment to the research and development necessary for the safe destruction of CFCs. Therefore, there is a minor effort to control CFCs, and perhaps this is a little too harsh, but I suspect no real commitment, if one looks at the record of the Government over the last four years, to other similar environmental areas.
As we look at this year's Estimates as well, we see a lot of words in terms of commitment to the environment, but no real commitment. Real commitment means you put your resources where your words are. That simply has not happened with the Estimates put forward by the Government this year. We see cuts in the commitment to inland waters, to fisheries, to atmospheric research, all those things which are part and parcel of the problem that this Bill purports to address; that is, the problem of CFCs, the problem of the deterioration, the destruction and, if we are not very careful, the imminent death of our atmosphere.
We see no commitment to municipal infrastructure. We all know that we need to do more to treat water supplies so that the circulation of water out of rivers and lakes and back into them is done in a way that does not
deteriorate those bodies of water. We have the technology now to improve the way we return water to the rivers, but we have poor and small municipalities unable to afford to implement that technology. Every province across this country is prepared to cost-share the improvement in the treatment of water, but this federal Government refuses to participate in it.
Looking back over what the Government has done with PCBs only reinforces my concern about its commitment to this Bill and to the protection of the atmosphere. Four years ago there was a PCB spill in Kenora. There was a great uproar. The Government was going to do something, but it was quietly forgotten for three years until St. Basile le Grand had a tragedy with PCBs fortunately just before an election. That jolted people into action. However, if we look at what has happened since, is there one federally-owned PCB site that has been cleaned up? Is there one federally-owned PCB deposit that has been destroyed? I think not.
Vehicles can still be purchased by the Government without emission standards. This Government has failed to use its power of spending to achieve the needed improvements. We will be speaking about that later today when we look at Bill C-3 to establish the Department of Industry, Science and Technology. But the Government has tremendous purchasing power amounting to billions of dollars every year to determine what products will be produced by the private sector for consumption in this country. Its very purchasing power gives it the ability to influence manufacturers to develop alternatives to CFCs. Yet it is not doing that. There is no policy within this Government to determine that we will not purchase products that are unsafe to the environment. There is no Minister who has the authority to ensure that such a policy is implemented.
This Bill ignores completely the fact that the CFCs we have already put into the environment will not cease doing their harm for another 16 years. The atmosphere will continue to deteriorate as a result of the products that we used yesterday. This is damage which is predictable, and it is treatable if we are committed to doing it. But we know that by continuing the use of CFCs, we continue their damage, not for tomorrow or for the 5,10 or 20 years we continue to use them, but for a full 16 years beyond that.
June 20, 1989

It is good that the Bill is here. I wish I felt that it were part of a real, ongoing and well understood commitment to consider our depletion of the earth's resources and our contribution to cleaning up the earth in everything we do. However, that is not what we have in front of us, that is not what I have seen from the Government in the last four years or in the last six months.
It has been said, and I guess it is a bit of a cliche, that all that is needed for evil to prevail is for good men to do nothing. I think it is a shame that the Government had to be forced by the courts to obey its own environmental guidelines. I thought that when we passed guidelines or laws to impose on other people it was because we believed in them and that we did not have to be forced by courts or anyone else to abide by them ourselves. I am a firm believer in "Do as I do, not as I say". It is a little hard for us to tell private industry to clean up if we are not prepared to clean up ourselves.
In passing this token legislation I challenge the Government to look at every aspect of our operation as a government and every aspect of the projects which we choose to fund here and abroad and consider what it is doing to the world that we are leaving to the next generation.
We need nationally enforceable standards and, more than that, we need a national and universal commitment by government to act on that which we all now know, that is, that unless we change our way of living we will not have a world to live in.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome an opportunity to make a comment in this debate today. As a Member, I object to the actions of certain Members who work extremely hard to make the environment into a very strongly partisan issue. It is clear to anyone that every Member in this House would do the most possible to ensure that our environment is indeed safe. I am sure that you, too, Mr. Speaker, would agree with that.
Canadians use about 2 per cent of the total world production of CFCs. Certainly we are part of the problem, but obviously not a huge part of the problem on a world-wide basis. From outside our borders Canada is looked upon as one of the leaders in establishing legislation and taking actions to control chlorofluorocar-bons. We need look back only as far as the Montreal Protocol to see the leadership which Canada has taken. We took part in that agreement and since that time it has been recognized that rather than only cutting by 50 per
Environmental Protection
cent we must basically eliminate the use of chlorofluoro-carbons in Canada.
The Government has put out a report for public perusal on the deadlines in various usage areas. I have no doubt that as soon as practical alternatives come along significant action will be taken and members of this Party, as much as Members of the Opposition, will work very hard to ensure that the necessary action is taken to control this very serious environmental problem which we, individually, have been watching for some time and on which we will demand action.
I am not sure that this particular Member mentioned, as others have, that we should take action on alternatives immediately. Quite frankly, some of those alternatives are not yet proven. What alternatives exist in the area of household refrigeration, for example, to convert household refrigeration appliances if we suddenly removed chlorofluorocarbons?

Mr. Speaker, it is fine to say that we all want to do our best. I cannot help wondering why the Government seems to believe that it should be left totally to market forces to develop these alternatives. Surely the Hon. Member must be aware of the need for government investment in research and technology that is to the benefit of all society. We cannot simply wait for the vagaries of the market. I did mention that the Government has an ability to influence the market in a positive way by refusing to purchase certain products. As long as we spend Canadian taxpayers' money on harmful products there is no incentive for anyone to develop alternatives. I challenge the Member to take that back to his caucus and suggest that there are more positive things that can be done.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to intervene in this debate very briefly. This is a Bill which we support. We support the objectives of the Bill in creating a legislative framework in which to enact regulations respecting the manufacture and expansion of CFCs and to implement the agreements of the Montreal protocol.
This is a very small Bill. Unfortunately, I take seriously the remarks of one of my Conservative colleagues that the environment is not really a partisan issue. It is an issue which is of much too great importance to debate merely on partisan grounds.
In this case, though, there are some things which should be said in response to the Government's proposition of this Bill at this time. It does indicate that the Environmental Protection Act was enacted last year in what was more or less a death bed conversion on the part of the Government to put together a major piece of environmental legislation in the final months before an election, when Decima told them it was the biggest issue on anyone's agenda in the real world.
We see a case of poor drafting in a statute that was hurriedly put together and needs to be amended before any other regulations have been proclaimed just in order to comply with the Montreal protocol which has been around for some years now.
I want to reflect on the importance of this Bill as a symbol of what we need to be doing here in this Chamber. In my few months here, we have debated the Free Trade Agreement with the United States. We have talked about the Budget and budget leaks. We have talked about the Constitution, things of great importance to many of us and to many Canadians.
June 20,1989

I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that what we are talking about today in this one-page Bill is the most important matter to come before us in the months of this Parliament.
What we have discovered in recent years, to our dismay, is how interrelated human activity truly is. For all those years when we, without a thought, used the CFC propellants in our aerosol cans, we never once thought of the long-term damage we were causing to the global environment. We have the evidence of the destruction of the ozone layer. It is not evidence which was easy to come by. According to an article in Time Magazine in 1987, they wrote:
For several years NASA's scientists failed to accept data on the Antarctic ozone hole that was before their eyes. The reason: Computers pre-screening data from monitoring satellites had been programmed to dismiss as suspicious presumably wild data showing a 30 per cent or greater drop in ozone levels. After British scientists reported the deficit in 1985, NASA went back to its computer records, finally recognizing that the satellite data had been showing the hole all along.
As we talk about the global crisis in the environment, Mr. Speaker, it is often that we hear these expositions of concern and worry dismissed as being panic-mongering or wony-mongering. Those dismissals have occurred before by elite scientists, as sophisticated and as well trained as those of NASA. They were proven to be wrong. Deterioration of the ozone is of special concern to those of us who find the sun somewhat difficult to bear as it is. The evidence is clear. I speak as someone with a bit of red hair and with two children with red hair. The evidence is clear that many of us are going to be prone to skin cancers in the years to come as a result of ozone deterioration. That is maybe the least of our problems.
The evidence is also clear that the agricultural product is going to be reduced. Productivity will be reduced as ozone deteriorates. Further, sea life is in peril as the plankton in some areas are killed by the ultraviolet rays. Onee the food chain is affected, what we have on our hands is a serious, serious problem in a world in which we are already having difficulty feeding our population. That is why I say that perhaps this little one-page Bill is the most important thing we have brought forward in this Parliament.
Environmental Protection
A few weeks ago, my 10-year old daughter came to me with a poem which she had written. She read it as a rap. It was kind of read to a beat. She gets up earlier than the rest of us and it was something which she sat down early in the morning on her own and produced. It was about the environment. She wrote a little poem about how we were messing things up.
I think the question that we all have to ask ourselves, as we carry on our duties as Canadian parliamentarians, is what do we say to the children? How do we explain to them that the world in which they are growing up is imperilled in a very basic fundamental way? Our abilities to sustain life are in peril because of our greed.
I think that this amendment is a good one. It is good that we are moving forward on the Montreal protocol. There are some criticisms that maybe the regulations should be sterner and maybe, as the Friends of the Earth in a press release issued today have said, we could reduce the CFC production more rapidly. We could make a greater contribution. I would urge the Government, if that is the case, to make every effort to expedite the reduction of CFC production.
That is not really the point. I think the point is that we have discovered in this global interrelatedness of our economy, of our energy policies, of our finance and of our environment, that we no longer live in a world separated by international boundaries. We are one another's neighbours.
We have a stake in the destruction of forests around the world. We have a stake in the economies of those countries whose poverty is driving them to destroy the very resources that they and the world needs in order to carry on. We have a stake in those countries who are so threatened by global warming that they may not continue to exist as nations if present trends continue.
I give you the example of the islands of the Maldives which will not exist in the world in 50 years' time if present global warming trends continue. I give you the example of the state of Egypt where 10 million of its people live at an B latitude less than one and one-half metres above sea level. If current global warming trends continue, that entire population will be forced to relocate. We, as Canadians, have a stake in these crucial world problems. We have contributed our part to the creation of these problems. We are called upon in our sophistication, in our higher education and in our wealth to contribute to their solutions not just within our own boundaries but world-wide.

June 20, 1989
Environmental Protection
I return to the question that I posed earlier somewhat rhetorically. What are we going to say to the children?

How to explain to the children of the world that we took too much-

That we were too greedy and that their future is in peril.

Member agree with me that that was one of the biggest scams for which this Government has ever been responsible in the sense that it went ahead with that without an environmental study, through a quick deal behind the doors, a backroom deal with the Premier and Deputy Premier of Saskatchewan with the consent, I would say, of the present Parliamentary Secretary who should think perhaps about shifting his portfolio away from environment. This, as the Hon. Member would know, caused the resignation of one of the senior staff members of the previous Minister of the Environment who blew the whistle on that gang of environmental crooks.
Would the Hon. Member comment on that? The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is heckling me. But surely the Canadian Federal Court showed what a scam the deal was.

I am putting the question, Mr. Speaker, if the Parliamentary Secretary would let me do so. He is very, very sensitive to this scam that he, Devine and Bemtsen made. The Federal Court of Canada had to overrule and caught them through some honest person in the Minister's office. It is a scam. Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. What we can be grateful for in this sorry history is the Federal Court of Canada and the decision it rendered.
The question points out the truth of what the Brund-tland Commission itself stated when it considered the problems that we have in trying to interrelate various aspects of policy making in a very complex economic environment. The Brundtland Commission in speaking of the challenges to link the aspects of policy making together in sustainable development stated:
The challenges are both interdependent and integrated, requiring comprehensive approaches and popular participation.
Yet most of the institutions facing those challenges tend to be independent, fragmented, working to relatively narrow mandates with closed decision processes.
Those responsible for managing natural resources and protecting the environment are institutionally separated from those responsible for managing the economy. The real world of interlocked economic and ecological systems will not change, the policies and institutions concerned must.

subtopic: INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I could, I would like to very briefly indicate our support for this amendment. We tried with several amendments in the legislative committee and before the House, amendments which were considered to extend the scope of the Bill unduly, to get the same sense of equity put into the legislation. We wanted a commitment
on the part of this ministry to have some kind of over all function with respect to economic equity in Canada.
In Canada, there are now essentially three quite disparate and often unco-ordinated agencies which are trying to achieve regional development. There is ACOA, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, which has one set of policies it is pursuing with respect to Atlantic Canada. There is the Western Diversification Office which has a completely different set of policies it is pursuing with respect to western Canada. As the legislation before us presently stands, there is also this ministry which will be taking responsibility for Ontario and Quebec. Talking of balkanization within a country, I think this is the most glaring example one could possibly see with respect to one of the most important functions of Government, its responsibility to achieve greater economic equity throughout the country.
If this motion is passed, it will have the effect of indicating the significance of this concern. It will not do as much as we would like to see done. We would like to see the responsibility clearly set out for the ministry to give some co-ordination to regional development efforts right across the country. In the absence of that, this motion would at least recognize that part of the responsibility of the Minister will be to work toward greater equity in economic opportunity throughout Canada.
Let me illustrate some of the problems that are coming up in the present situation. At the moment, the constraints which have been imposed on ACOA have led it to focus its assistance very much on small-scale business in Atlantic Canada. I personally think that makes sense, but at the same time, the Minister responsible for western diversification, when he testified recently before the Standing Committee, Industry, Science and Technology, Regional and Northern Development, indicated that he himself was putting the emphasis on larger scale projects in western Canada. In fact, the great bulk of money provided through his office for western diversification has gone to large scale projects. June 20, 1989

Motion No. 4
That Bill C-3, an Act to establish the Department of Industry,
Science and Technology, to repeal the Department of Regional

June 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
Industrial Expansion Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be amended in Clause 8 by adding immediately after line 27 at page 4 the following:
"(i) develop, implement, and promote national policies to foster economic development that is environmentally sustainable;"
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion to amend the Bill to create the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, is intended to bring within the provisions of that Bill the requirement that the Minister, in exercising his duties as Minister, develop, implement and promote national policies to foster economic development that is environmentally sustainable.
This amendment goes to the very core of what the Government has been stating about its interest and concern in the environment. It goes to the core of the Prime Minister's praise for the work of the Brundtland Commission. This amendment seeks to take this Department of Government, which is a key economic Department, and put within it the responsibility to look to sustainable development as a key aspect of economic policy. This is entirely consistent with the proposals of the Brundtland Commission. I submit that it is entirely consistent with what the Government has been stating. Remember the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, wherein the Government proclaimed that the environment was to be one of its first priorities?
I have a series of press clippings here: "More priority for environment is promised by new minister"; "Environment No. 1, Bouchard says"; "Environment comes first in new projects: Bouchard"; and "Environment to get top priority, minister says". This is to be the top priority. An article in The Globe and Mail on February 1, states in part:
The new federal Environment Minister, Lucien Bouchard-said the new government's thinking is in keeping with the concept of sustainable development: that the prevention of present and future harmful environmental effects has equal priority with other economic and social goals.
This is consistent with the recommendations of the Brundtland Commission. I also wish to quote from the Brundtland Commission report which states:
In the past, responsibility for environmental matters has been placed in environmental ministries and institutions that often have had little or no control over destruction caused by agricultural, industrial, urban development, forestry, and transportation policies and practices. Society has failed to give the responsibility for preventing environmental damage to the 'sectoral' ministries and agencies whose policies cause it. Thus our environmental management practices have focused largely upon after-the-fact repair of damage: reforestation, reclaiming desert lands, rebuilding
urban environments, restoring natural habitats, and rehabilitating wild lands.
The ability to anticipate and prevent environmental damage will require that the ecological dimensions of policy be considered at the same time as the economic, trade, energy, agricultural, and other dimensions.
The Science Council of Canada in its report entitled Environmental Peacekeepers makes the same point. Again, I quote:
Global environmental deterioration has been spawned in large measure by science and technology applied to unsustainable economic growth and development in the industrialized countries. It is worsening as those Third World countries that can do so accelerate their economic development in order to raise their living standards-
The role of science and technology in undoing the global ecological crisis-if it is to be undone at all-is of paramount importance.
The Science Council of Canada goes on to recommend that the Department of Industry, Science and Technology take a leading role in the environmental renewal that the world calls for us to have.
This is a challenge to the Government. This is its commitment to live by the intent of the Brundtland Report. This is its opportunity to embark on an exciting adventure. Let us say now to Canada and the world that our key economic development Department of the Government of Canada is going to take into its heart and soul concerns about the environment.
I know what the response in the legislative committee on similar amendments was. It was: "Well, there is an environmental policy committee of Cabinet to review these things". Is that not the Canadian way, Mr. Speaker? We will turn it over to a committee. Committees are well known for the types of decisions they make.
Let us take environmental concerns and put them under the responsibility of the Minister who is going to carry out policies whose very implications could be threatening to the environment. That is where it belongs. That is the challenge to the Government.

Mr. Speaker, first, I want to say a brief word of congratulation to the Hon. Member for Ottawa South (Mr. Manley) for having taken this very fine initiative. Second, I wish to say that if any Member of the Progressive Conservative Party were to vote against the amendment now proposed by the Hon. Member,, they in substance and in spirit would be voting against their own Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), their own Speech from the Throne and statements made at home and abroad by their own Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
June 20,1989

I will explain to you why, Mr. Speaker, I say that. The amendment being proposed reads simply that the mandate of this Department should also "develop, implement, and promote national policies to foster economic development that is environmentally sustainable".
What the Hon. Member for Ottawa South is proposing is what the Prime Minister proposed at the United Nations in June of last year. Do the Progressive Conservative Members in the House want to vote against what their own Prime Minister said abroad? If that is not enough, would they want to deny a major paragraph contained in the Speech from the Throne which states: "My Government will pursue sustainable development as a major thrust in the policy development of this Government in this Parliament"? Is that not what it states in the Speech from the Throne?
On April 27, when the Minister of Finance delivered his speech in this House he, in his own words, said he also wants to have economic development that is consistent with sustainable development.
The Minister repeats the old chestnut that his colleague the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Andre) brought up in committee when he said: "Oh well, do not do that because the development and environment Department should do it". That thinking belongs to the caveman. It has been put aside at a number of places where Canada participates and in organizations of which Canada is a member, namely, the OECD, the United Nations, and through two members of the Brundtland Commission-everywhere we have agreed to the principle that we should now integrate the economy with the environment.
We have even reached the point of adopting and sponsoring the notion that the environment ought to be made the responsibility of every Department. Now is the opportunity to practise the theory that has been embraced by the Prime Minister at home and abroad, by the Minister of Finance and by some Members of Cabinet who attempt to do it and, quite understandably so, within the realm and powers given to Cabinet.
Industry, Science and Technology
What the Hon. Member for Ottawa South is proposing is really an additional step, but a very practical one. The first practical opportunity to implement this practical step within the Government's structure is by saying that the formation of a new Department which, among other responsibilities, has the responsibility to ensure that the fostering of economic development be also environmentally sustainable.
It is a beautiful amendment. It is a great opportunity for Members on the Government side to practise what their Prime Minister preaches abroad and at home, and also what some of their own colleagues in the environment committee have been saying for weeks and months now. They also support and quote Madam Brundtland, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa South has just done. It would be a contradiction of their own polity, of their own credo, of their own statements and beliefs if they were to vote against this amendment.
This is where the political crunch is. We are anxiously awaiting the moment when you call the vote, Mr. Speaker, to see that there is consistency in the beliefs of the Progressive Conservative Government when it comes to sustainable development.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa South is offering Members opposite a unique opportunity to practise what they preach. It is not good enough to go to the United Nations and make a great declaration. It is not good enough to go to The Hague as the Prime Minister did in March and make another declaration. It is not a matter of a declaration here. It is a matter of putting into legislation a very sound and basic principle, one that is being proposed by the Hon. Member for Ottawa South. We congratulate him.

down river within the St. Lawrence. If we are going to recognize the motherhood principles within this clause, surely it makes equally as much sense to recognize the importance of our environment.

-a duty is placed upon the decision maker, insofar as is reasonably possible, to appreciate fully the significance of and the foundation for the various individual or group interests.

Industry, Science and Technology

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the fact that this motion is even here for debate is a crying condemnation of the Government's real commitment to sustainable development. It is in fact a blatant demonstration that Members of the Government on the committee that considered this legislation do not even understand what sustainable development is. They failed to understand that the whole message of the Brundtland Commission, the whole message of sustainable development is that the economy and the environment are inextricably linked. We cannot continue to use the earth's resources, deplete those resources, to return them to the earth filthy, to the air filthy, to the water filthy, or to use them up faster than they can be replenished and hope to have an economy that will continue to provide us with the goods and services that we require.
We cannot afford to export the kind of wasteful, destructive, economic activity that we have enjoyed in the developed world to those countries that are just now developing. That is the whole message: the economy and the environment cannot be separated. That is why the motion of my colleague from Ottawa South (Mr. Manley) is one that should enjoy the unanimous consent of this House.
How can one foster tourism, foster entrepreneurship, foster competitiveness and not look at the resources that we draw from the world to create that entrepreneurship, to draw those tourists, to feed the industries, to support the competitiveness? How can we fail to preserve those very things that drive the economy? Therefore, how can the Minister himself say that the mandate of this department is developing economic strength? Does he really not understand and does every Member sitting across the aisle not understand that the strength is based on the resources of the earth. If you do not use them in a way that ensures their preservation, you do not have resources on which to build your economy. It is an integral part of the mandate of this department. It must be, or there will be no reason for this department to exist.
Far more important, it is essential that this concept be absorbed into every department within Government. At the Environment Committee, we have been discussing how to achieve this at meeting after meeting. Here is our first opportunity to do so.
The Minister responsible for the Department of Industry, Science and Technology (Mr. Andre) said that the Department of the Environment has the responsibility for those things. He was talking about sustainable development. He said that this amendment and spreading the responsibility for sustainable development to other departments do not contribute to better Government. That is precisely what must happen. It must become the responsibility of everybody who works for Government, everybody who directs any program of Government, to ensure that the work they are carrying out is in conformity with our commitment to the future of the world. We owe it in fact to the quarter of a million of people who work for the Government of Canada to make sure that they have that message. There are citizens out there who are concerned, as your polls tell you, that our Government, and we individually, take action to preserve the environment.
June 20, 1989

There are citizens who want to know what they can do in their workplace to contribute to a better world. If that leadership is not there in every department, from the top down, they will not get that message. We will go on spending over $100 billion a year in our procurement of goods and services, on products that are damaging to the environment instead of using our purchasing power to influence what the market produces and how safe it is.
If the Government is wise, it will spread that influence to other public spending. The provincial governments across this country spend that much and more every year. The municipal governments collectively spend 25 per cent more than the Government of Canada. What a magnificent economic tool to harness and foster the growth of environmentally safe products.
Another thing that rejecting this amendment does to the mandate of the Department, in fact to the responsibilities of the Minister, is to ignore some very excellent opportunities for economic development, for economic growth, and for competitiveness for new small businesses. One of the key opportunities in the next few decades will be for nations that know enough to see the problems of the world and develop solutions to them. Canada is ideally situated, both climatologically and environmentally and in terms of our stage of development, to be one of the world leaders in developing solutions to environmental problems. There are few countries in the world that have the capacity, the natural strength to do it as this country has. If sustainable development is not part of the responsibility of this Department, then that opportunity will be missed.
The question of sustainable development of environmental consciousness is not a little jewel to be put in a box and brought out for press conferences and to show our international friends on international junkets. Yet that seems to be the impression of the Minister who said in committee that "the Government's direction is to want an economy that is of high quality in terms of sustainable development, to preserve and enhance the environment that provides for things that are not immediately of tangible value but have some higher values; poetiy, music, what have you." The Minister obviously fails to understand that we are talking about the survival of the world and of human life in this world. These are
Industry, Science and Technology
not nice little extras to have, they are essential to human life. If we try to treat the environment like a jewel that we put in a box and trot out and admire and flash around when we want to look good, we will find that what we have in fact is a Pandora's box.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this concept. I am not a member of the Environment Committee as is the Member who just spoke, or of the technological committees of which Members have been speaking. However, I have a great deal of interest in the environment.
About 15 years ago I was associated with the Berger Inquiry on the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. We went to examine the social, economic and environmental implications on the people of the North of the building of the massive megaproject. Before we really started the inquiry, I had the honour to go with Judge Berger to New York to the United Nations. We went to see the United Nations environmental people to find out what other countries had done. As the Member from Ottawa West (Mrs. Catterall) who previously spoke said, Canada had to show the lead. We were surprised to find out that no other country had ever looked at the environmental implications of the building of a megaproject before the project was built. A lot of them could see it afterwards but no one had looked at it before. Canada was a pioneer in this.
I have watched this environment issue develop over the years. This is an interesting motion, it is to amend the Bill to add "develop, implement and promote national policies to foster economic development that is environmentally sustainable". The Brundtland Commission speaks, I believe, of sustainable development. What is sustainable development? I am a layman, not a member of these committees and not one directly involved in environmental issues. I know that sustainable development has been defined by some Members here today but it still seems to me like nailing jelly to the wall.

June 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
Let us be honest, what is sustainable development? I talked to someone who looked at all Canadian government programs to try to find examples of sustainable development under the widely defined terms of development that is good for the future, that does not destroy our resources but keeps them for our children and our children's children. That is much the way in which native people speak of developing resources. This is the western liberal technological equivalent to the native holistic view of being at home with the forest and the land and keeping them for their children. The same thing is luckily and finally happening here for us and it may be the key to saving this planet.
Given that broad definition of sustainable development, I asked people whether we could find any existing government programs which fit into it. We found one program, and that says a lot for what past and present governments have done. The program we found was the Fish Habitat Program developed during Mr. Speaker Fraser's tenure as Environment Minister, I am pleased to say. That program provides for the replacement of fish habitat that is destroyed by a construction project.
For example, let's say you were going to add a runway to the airport in Vancouver. You would have to prove, first, that that is a productive construction approach, that it would add to our productivity. One could easily make that argument, two runways would contribute to more economic development and so on.
The second aspect is that you have to replace the fish habitat. If the runway goes into the Fraser River, for example, you would have to find alternate habitats. The development would have to be sustainable to the surrounding environment, specifically the fish habitat. That is an example of sustainable development. The developers may have to find more fish habitat in another part of the river and develop it. That is the only program we could find, of all the programs of the federal Government. That says a lot, doesn't it?
The second point I would like to raise is that we need some way of measuring sustainable development. It is all very well to say that the Minister shall develop, implement and promote national policies to foster economic development that is environmentally sustainable. How do you measure it? Well, that can be done as well. I
understand that there are some people in the World Bank working on new ways of measuring sustainable development. In the 1930s we had to invent new ways of looking at the world when Keynesian economics came along and so on. They invented Gross National Product. As an example, Canada's GNP grew by 5 per cent last year, our goods and services. Had we cut down and logged all the trees in Canada, our Gross National Product might have grown by 9 per cent, but we would have lost the trees so we would not really have made progress. Certainly that development would not be sustainable. I understand that they are working on a measurement to measure sustainable development.
That will mean we have to do an inventory of all our resources. Then we will have to measure how much we use them without replacing them. This is going to be a very interesting figure. We will be able to set targets. We can set a target for the year 2050, or a target for the year 2080 or whatever. We can tell whether we are doing development that is sustainable on our planet or whether we are losing the resources of our planet.
I think I have spoken enough on this. I just find it a fascinating, interesting area for all of us in the House. It is an area which is hard to define. It is worth supporting this motion. However, let us not kid ourselves, we still have a lot of work to do. It is all very well to say that yes, we develop, implement and promote national policies to foster economic development that is environmentally sustainable. We have a lot of work to do to define what that is, project by project and inventory by inventory of every part and every sector in the economy from forest to fish to minerals and so on.
We have just taken, as one Chinese politician once said, the first step in a march of a million miles. It is going to be a long march to get to what we actually mean by sustainable development. At least this is a start.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is particularly appropriate that we are speaking about this particular amendment to Bill C-23 on the same day that we have been dealing with the amendment in respect of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
June 20, 1989

As has been very ably pointed out by my colleagues, the Member for Ottawa South (Mr. Manley), the Member for Ottawa West (Mrs. Catterall) and the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), the amendment which has been proposed by my colleague is in keeping with the spirit of sustainable development which we thought was launched by Brundtland and was embraced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). No less than the Prime Minister. We heard the Prime Minister in the House vaunting the work of Gro Harlem Brundtland and vaunting it to the point where he was very pleased to have accepted the award which he took in Washington, et cetera. This is the first time that outside of the context of the Environment Committee we have an opportunity at a departmental level to incorporate in the raison d'Etre of a newly established Department. We have the capacity to build in the implementation and promotion of national policies to foster economic development which is environmentally sustainable.
Anybody who took the time to read our common future would understand that for any minimal accomplishment of sustainable development it has to be applied across the board in various Departments. I cannot believe the statement of the Minister, who stated that: "So regarding adding that clause, this is the clause that has been proposed with respect to sustainable development. The recommendation simply does not fit directly with this Department. I suggest we have a cleaner"-it is a rather Freudian point, Mr. Speaker-"more reasonable approach to things, leaving the responsibility for the environment with that Department."
Surely, the whole purpose of the Brundtland report was to wake up the world to the fact that we cannot departmentalize environmental questions. The question of sustainable development must permeate every decision made by the Government insofar as where we promote industry, where we develop our science policy and where we in fact spend the money that would lead to a policy of industry, science and technology.
In this particular case, we are repealing the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion Act. We are basically saying where we are going to put our financial clout over the next number of years. That decision
Industry, Science and Technology
cannot be made in a vacuum, without putting the environmental questions in context.
Every single thing which we do in this House of Commons, and every single Act which is carried out by Parliament has a potential environmental impact.
Next week, July 1, is Canada Day. At this point, the National Capital Commission, which is responsible for the promotion of Canada Day activities on Parliament Hill, will be committing environmental folly by releasing
10,000	balloons into the environment.
The Province of Nova Scotia has already banned the release of balloons because they recognize that the effect of a burst balloon on the ecosystem is such that when, for example, fish, sea whales, sea turtles and whales eat rubber, which is the product of the burst balloons, they can actually have their normal eating habits impaired because they think they are full when they have basically swallowed a piece of a balloon. It sounds somewhat comical, Mr. Speaker, but it is a reflection that every decision which we make, whether it is as minor as organizing a celebration to release balloons on Parliament Hill, or as major as a decision to proceed with the hydroelectric project cannot be taken without environmental consideration.
I have here in my hand a copy of the hydroelectric resistance program which was produced by the Grand Council of the Crees of Quebec. It is a voluminous document. It points out the crying need for a federal environmental assessment in respect of a potential decision to proceed with a second phase of the development of the hydroelectric project on James Bay.
In fact, this particular Department, the Department which we are about to launch, oftentimes the Department of Industry, Science and Technology will put forward financial backing for these types of projects. Whether it be financial backing by way of an interest-free loan to Lavalin to go off and develop a light rapid transit system in a Third World country, or whether it be in relation to a specific regional development project in Canada, there are potentially environmental implications.
If we look at the specific decision now, for example, in the Province of Nova Scotia, to proceed with a new technology for the extraction of energy from coal, that again involves environmental implications.

June 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
The amendment which was moved by my colleague, the Member for Ottawa South and supported, I might add, by a Conservative Member of Parliament who recognizes that it simply embraces and endorses all of the promotion of the environment which we have been talking about since the arrival of Brundtland, surely any Member in his or her right mind who would not support this motion cannot call themselves an environmentalist. I heard the-

-the Hon. Member for Gaspe (Mr. Marin) this afternoon, when we were talking about protecting the environment, accused me of being a politician, of playing petty politics with the environment. He accused me of petty politics. Today, Mr. Speaker, we have a bill and a motion that can be supported by all Members. All we ask, Mr. Speaker, is to include the comment made by Mrs. Brundtland. The Prime Minister talks a lot about Brundtland. He is crazy about Brundtland. All we ask is to have the legislation reflect the Brundtland proposals, in other words, when we create the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, we recognize the fact that the department's terms of reference should include to develop, implement and promote national policies to foster economic development that is environmentally sustainable. If we want to be known as environmentalists who do not play petty politics with the environment, then we have no choice but to vote for this very effective, very short and very sustainable amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-South (Mr. Manley).
Instead of pointing the accusing finger and saying that Members are playing politics, I wish Hon. Members would realize that Canadians are sick and tired of politicians who talk about policies but are not prepared to put those same words in the Bill and the legislation.
Mr. Speaker, do I have a little more time or just ten seconds?
We all know that this Bill, this amendment is an opportunity to incorporate, not just the environmental spirit but also the Kind of legislation that will protect us. I want to make two points with respect to this Bill in front of us now to establish the Department of Industry, Science and Technology which represents a further step in the process of this country turning its back on equitable regional development. I think that it is an extremely unfortunate set of steps that we have taken.
If we go back to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, there we had a ministry which had as its single and sole purpose the expansion of regional development throughout this country. That was something we, in this Party, have always seen as an essential commitment that Ottawa should be making to all of the people of this country, a commitment which also should be made by the provinces. DREE itself was done away with. Then we had the establishment of DRIE, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. Within DRIE we had two functions together. We had the function of industrial development for the entire country and we had the function of regional development for the country as a whole put together.
June 20, 1989

There was some serious difficulty in trying to mesh these two differing functions together within one ministry. It functioned and it operated within two separate sections of the ministry. One section dealt with industrial development and the other dealt with regional development. With this Bill we have the elimination of any national commitment to regional development within our country. If this Bill is passed as it stands there will not be a single ministry within this Government that has the commitment to see that there is fairness and equal opportunity in different regions within Canada.
If we were Luxemburg, even The Netherlands, or Switzerland, this might not be something for us to be concerned about but we are not. We are an incredibly large diverse country with remarkable differences in terms of the economic base of livelihood from which people start.
An exciting thing about being a Member of Parliament is the chance to see many different parts of our country. It is both exciting and stimulating, but it is also terribly distressing to see in central British Columbia, for instance, unemployment rates of 15 per cent, 16 per cent and 17 per cent, to see in northern Saskatchewan unemployment rates of 13 per cent, 14 per cent and 15 per cent, to see in parts of northern Ontario unemployment rates of a similar magnitude and to see in Atlantic Canada, especially in parts of Atlantic Canada, unemployment rates that are at real levels once you take into account where people really stand with regard to the labour force. Real unemployment rates are often over 50 per cent.
People from Newcastle, New Brunswick have told me of unemployment rates in their part of the country in real terms that reach over 50 per cent. The same is true in parts of the outports of Newfoundland. In fact, there are parts of Newfoundland where one finds unemployment rates in which the percentage of people who are at work is significantly less than the percentage of people who would like to be within the work force. One can see the same thing in other parts of Atlantic Canada.
Industry, Science and Technology
We see the same thing happening in the Province of Quebec. In some parts of Quebec the unemployment rate is far too high for a developed country like ours.
In the Eastern Townships, for instance, in the textile and clothing sectors, the unemployment rate can be as high as 30 or 35 per cent.
What we are seeing, Mr. Speaker, is not just unacceptably high levels of unemployment, we are seeing a situation where many workers cannot find jobs, and as result, they decide that they better stay home because there are no jobs available.

That is the reality of regional disadvantages which exist in parts of Canada. Since the Government has not been prepared to bring amendments to this Bill, amendments which would give the Department some responsibility to co-ordinate and work toward regional fairness, it is necessary to keep the Regional Industrial Expansion Act as it presently stands.
