speakeroldname: Mr. Howard McCurdy (Windsor-Lake St. Clair) moved:
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSFER PAYMENTS POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should restore funds cut from federal transfer payments to the provinces for post-secondary education and complete an agreement with the provinces to provide assured levels of funding commensurate with the increased costs of universities' operations and the need to enhance the availability of resourceful humans for economic development and full employment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it has become almost trite these days to observe that Canada, for a force, must shift from a resource based economy to a knowledge based economy if it is to compete in the new economic circumstances that exist in the world. It has been said, and it is true, that we can no longer depend upon our forests, our land, our minerals, and the fish from the sea to sustain this modern nation in present circumstances.
This was an observation that underscored a remark made by the Prime Minister back in 1983, which I can merely paraphrase. He said that if there was not a dramatic improvement in Canada's performance in the area of research and development, Canada would play in the minor leagues of the competition in this world in economic terms. Just yesterday the Prime Minister made a similar remark. He said:
Either we meet the challenge of competitiveness and ride the crest
of the technology wave into the 21st century or we exhaust ourselves
in the rip-tide of history, fading inexorably backwards.
So far all we have managed is to be inundated with rhetoric while there exists a virtual drought in action. The Prime Minister, I note, made another remark. He said that a recent survey of 13 countries ranked Canadian high school students eleventh in biology, eleventh in physics, and twelfth in chemistry, "the very subjects on which the knowledge industry depends".
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the deplorable performance of our high school students cited by the Prime Minister is really a reflection of the quality and the character of the teachers that we are producing in universities which have fallen into a disgraceful state.
Right now in this country we are spending something in the order of $13,000 on an average per student while in the United States the average expenditure per student is $20,000. That is an average. Canadians recognize, as a matter of fact Canadians consistently observe that the quality of education in the United States is so much worse than ours. This is just a recognition that there are some states, Mississippi, Alabama and so on, in which the quality of post-secondary education or education at any level does not meet the quality which we think exists in Canada. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that those figures which I cited are averages. In fact, in some states of the United States four to five times as much money is spent per student as is spent in Canada.
Beginning just after World War II the federal Government began to provide financing for post-secondary education in the forms of grants to veterans. Then in the year 1966 or 1967 the federal Government entered into an agreement with the provinces to provide 50-50 sharing for the funding of post-secondary education. This worked out quite well, and I think that many of us in this House will recall that this was the most significant period in terms of developing accessibility and building the university and college system in Canada. These were halcyon days from 1967 until 1977.
In 1977 the then Liberal Government negotiated with the provinces something which is still called Established Programs Financing that covers transfers to the provinces for both health and post-secondary education. Subsequently legislation has been passed which assures that those portions of EPF which are allocated to health indeed go to health. However, since 1977 there has been
June 20, 1989

no assurance that funds provided by the federal Government for post-secondary education indeed go to post-secondary education and that those funds are matched in any way by the provinces.
The situation as it has evolved since then is such that the vast bulk of the cost of post-secondary education, both in colleges and universities, is paid for by the federal Government. It is notable in that context that only the Province of Quebec matches the federal contribution for post-secondary education on the 50-50 basis which characterized the decade after 1967.
Not only has there not been an equivalent contribution from the provinces, there have been cut-backs in the amounts transferred from the federal Government to the provincial Government for post-secondary education.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSFER PAYMENTS POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext: Be careful how you say it.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSFER PAYMENTS POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
This has occurred as a result of decisions taken by both the Liberal Government and the Conservative Government. I know that to resort to history on this is bothersome, but let us understand what we are talking about here. The undertaking in 1977 was that the growth in post-secondary education transfer payments from the federal Government were to grow in the same measure, based on three-year averaging, as the growth in the Gross Domestic Product. That applied to health transfers and to transfers for post-secondary education.
In 1982-83 the Liberal Government imposed the 6 per cent and 5 per cent rule, which was broadly applied to wages and so on, to be transferred to post-secondary education costing the system something in the order of $400 million over that period of time. Then in 1986 the Conservative Government, arguing as my colleague across the way just did, did not cut post-secondary education by $1.6 billion from the period from 1986 to 1991. It just cut the expectations of the system by $1.6 billion in respect to post-secondary education.
We know that those on the other side will use whatever semantic arguments they may choose to try to convince themselves of the obvious, that is, that the undertaking made by the federal Government to the
Post-Secondary Education
provinces, to post-secondary education, and to the youth of this country was reneged upon.
As if it were not enough, even as every significant examiner of the situation in this country with respect to post-secondary education said that there was going to have to be an increase in expenditures, this Government has proceeded in the last Budget to impose yet further cuts, which beginning in 1991 will accumulate over the next five years an additional cut of $1 billion in transfer payments for post-secondary education.
My colleague across the way will say: "Oh, well we didn't cut; we are just not going to give them as much". When we have a system which between 1977 and 1987 occasioned a real decrease in real dollars of 10 per cent while student enrolment rose by 30 per cent, I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that is a cut. It certainly is a failure to fulfil a promise. It is a failure to respond to the needs in this country which everyone by now recognizes.
It is an absolute outrage that in a period of time when this country should be developing the means to respond to the demands of an international knowledge based industry the Government should be cutting expenditures for post-secondary education, while at the same time refusing to increase expenditures for research and development.
There are classes in our universities with as many as
5,000	students. There are seminars which are supposed to be for small groups, intimate, close, and Socratic in which as many as 50 students are expected to benefit from the intimate examination of knowledge and are intended to learn.
There is not a criterion of economic success with respect to the knowledge based economy in which we do not finish last or near last. Every institution, every commission, every committee within this House, at the federal level, at the provincial level, or anywhere has recognized that there is going to have to be a change. There are going to have to be substantial increases in expenditures for post-secondary education and the mess that exists at this time, in which the federal Government and the provincial Governments dispute how much of a share each is paying, has to end.

June 20, 1989
Post-Secondary Education
It has to end. If it does not end, we are going to deny not only our future prospects for economic growth but opportunity to thousands of students who want nothing else but the opportunity to build a particular vision of Canada which is not borrowed from elsewhere.
What is the solution to this? The solution has been clear. It has been debated repeatedly in this House. It has been debated in the Committee on Science and Technology. It has been debated in the Committee of the Secretary of State. It has been debated in the Senate. It has been considered by the National Advisory Board for Science and Technology. It has been considered by the Bovey report. It has been considered by the A1 Johnson report. It has been considered by so many people that even this Government ought to be able to understand what is necessary.
What is necessary is for the urgent call of a First Ministers Conference. They should not be allowed out of a locked room until they have agreed on a basis for the shared funding of post-secondary education which will ensure that both levels pay their share. Nothing else will do. We can no longer burden ourselves with petty jurisdictional disputes while our country and our youth suffer. They are suffering now, and they will suffer yet more. To suggest that the burden of a deficit is going to be an overwhelming burden is ridiculous as compared to the kind of burden which will be their inheritance if we do not begin to catch up.
It is impertinent nonsense for the Prime Minister to condemn our schools for their failure to produce the level of literacy in science, as he did, while at the same time refuse to do what is necessary and to fulfil the promise he has made.
When we stand before you, Mr. Speaker, to support this motion, it is very simple and very clear. The funds which this Government has cut should be restored. The deficit and the allocation of funds to post-secondary institutions will breed a deficit so huge in the future, an intellectual deficit, an economic deficit, and a deficit in jobs, that it will be far more serious than a self-created deficit which this Government seeks to defend at odds with itself, as it has continued to do.
Second, in recognizing the mutual responsibility of both the federal and provincial Governments, they should, as I said before, through the calling of a First Ministers Conference come to an immediate resolution of this issue. Otherwise the future will look, indeed, as if this country in the economic league will be playing not Class C but sand lot.

speechtext: Bush league.

speechtext:
Bush league is too high for what will result from the continued travel along this route. Let me say another thing which is not contained in this motion-but which I think is necessary. This country has no policy focus with respect to any level of education.
I do not think that there is anyone who does not understand that there is something wrong when one-quarter of our population is functionally illiterate. This does not reflect the role of universities. This reflects the role of the elementary and secondary institutions. All need some policy focus. All need initiatives which will relate the nature of our curriculum at the lower levels and the functions of the institutions at the higher levels with our economic priorities, as well as our social priorities. This is a country in which the economic imperatives do not outweigh and ought not to outweigh the social imperatives. We should develop the necessary models without encroaching upon particular jurisdictions which will permit our institutions of education at all levels to provide the kind of knowledge that will enable all Canadians to exercise the kinds of creativity and the intelligence of which Canadians given the opportunity are capable so that we will be seen as not only an economic success but a social success and a model for the world. It is almost too late.
I know, Mr. Speaker, by the way in which you are posing your hands that you are concerned and anxious for the Government to get on with it. I am sure that you are waiting to hear a positive response with respect to the required initiatives.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSFER PAYMENTS POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was listening to the Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party, and what struck me in nearly all the speeches by Opposition Members, whether they represent the New Democratic Party or the Liberal Party of Canada, what struck me was the constant and increasing demand for money, without considering the broader context of our national economy. Money is needed for post-secondary education, for the provinces, for this and for that, but no one bothers to consider this country's main problem, and that problem is what we refer to as the national debt and the deficit. Mr. Speaker, as you know, our national debt has now reached $320 billion. This year, the annual deficit will increase by an additional $6 billion because of rising interest rates. However, since 1984, the Progressive Conservative Party has done a tremendous job of controlling and dealing with our national debt. In 1984, the debt increased 24 per cent. In 1989, we have managed to keep the increase down to 10 per cent. Even at that, we
June 20, 1989

still have this national debt which is increasing and we have a deficit that is still too high. We hope, and I believe we have taken the necessary steps to bring the deficit down to approximately $16 billion by 1993-94.
The last Budget, like all other Budgets, was a serious exercise in restraint, and I think the Minister of Finance is to be commended. We managed to reduce spending and programs, and we raised income tax and certain other taxes so that this year, the Government will be able to collect $5 billion and next year, an additional $9 billion, which will be used to reduce our annual deficit and control our national debt, a process that is already underway.
Mr. Speaker, when we consider the specific issue the Hon. Member was discussing this evening, and I am referring to transfer payments to the provinces, there are, in fact, two distinct types of payments. I am referring to equalization payments and so-called established programs financing. As you know, Mr. Speaker, equalization payments are made to certain provinces on the basis of their revenues and according to a pre-established formula. The April Budget in no way interfered with equalization payments. We are not decreasing the amount allocated for established program financing, but we are reducing the percentage increase, which is something else. As a result, established program financing in 1988-89 was $18.7 billion; in 1989-90, it is $19.8 billion; and in 1990-91, it will be $20.8 billion. So we see that the annual amount of established program financing given by the federal Government to the provinces is increasing. We only reduced the percentage increase. Equalization payments in 1988-89 were $6.9 billion; in 1989-90, they are $7.3 billion; and in 1990-91, they will be almost $7 billion. Once again, Mr. Speaker, you see the annual increase provided.
I will go further, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the best way to look at how the Canadian Government operates is in percentage terms. For 1989-90, we will spend-the Canadian Government will spend $103.5 billion; 10 per cent of that is grants for businesses; 10.8 per cent is for national defence; 4.6 per cent is for Crown corporations;
Post-Secondary Education
2.4 per cent is aid for developing countries; 31.5 per cent is for individual Canadians, for old age security, etc.; and 23.2 per cent is for the provinces, which means that 23.2 per cent of the money spent by the Canadian Government goes to the provinces in cash. And to that, I must add $10.5 billion in fiscal transfers. A total of $34.4 billion annually goes from the federal Government, the Government of Canada, to the ten provinces and two territories.
Mr. Speaker, that's not peanuts! These astronomical figures, I think, show what this Government does for Canadians' welfare and also the interest the Conservative Government has in every province giving its citizens the goods and services to which every resident of every province is entitled.
You see, Mr. Speaker, I could go on giving figures and point out among other things that with respect to the increase in established programs financing from 1979-80 to 1983-84 we are talking about $54 billion. From 1984-85 to 1988-89, Mr. Speaker, the amount was $83 billion. And our estimates for the years 1989-90 to 1993-94 amount to $107 billion, almost $108 billion for established programs financing alone, funds which will be paid by the federal Government to the ten provinces and the two territories.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest these figures speak for themselves. However, we must not lose sight of the April 1989 Budget which urged all Canadians to tighten their belts and keep in mind the current economic situation of the country. The potential is there, whether we are talking about raw materials, labour or skills, but all that cannot be put to contribution and create jobs if we are saddled with a serious economic problem, if our country is debt-ridden. You know how things were, Mr. Speaker, because you were a Member of the House when interest rates peaked at 22 per cent and you made some comments about that situation. From the outset we had-we still have-to get a handle on threatening inflation. For the first time in years, Mr. Speaker, we have an inflation rate of 5 per cent. This is why we need interest rates to stem the current inflationary trends, and this will automatically guarantee that the country will steer the same course it has been following over the past four years.

June 20, 1989
Post-Secondary Education
I am thinking of the kind of job creation we have seen over the last four years, due to this Progressive Conservative Government's sound management.
Within that overall context, Mr. Speaker, the Budget had to make difficult choices in terms of tax increases, of certain program cuts, and also in terms of transfers or rather of increase of moneys to be transferred once more by the Canadian Government to each and every province.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe the motion now before us does not recognize the economic reality across the land. And when it comes to the Budget, when it comes to managing a nation like Canada, we should not look at a small square only, a single card, because there are 52 different cards in a deck!
We must therefore look at the overall Canadian picture, before making our choices. This is what the April Budget did. I see you are signalling my time is up, so let me conclude by stating that the motion in my view is not warranted within the overall Canadian economic situation.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSFER PAYMENTS POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am. pleased to rise to speak on this motion. It provides the Government a wonderful opportunity to correct its ways, to give renewed hope to our youth, to women, to the poor, to the unemployed, to older workers and to all Canadians who wish to upgrade and improve their skills and education at a university, a community college or a number of various other sources which increase literacy. This provides an opportunity for Canadians to become more competitive, to contribute more to Canadian society, to find a more secure future for themselves and for their children.
This is not only an opportunity for renewed hope but also an opportunity to ensure that education, training, retraining and research and development become the cornerstones of our economic development, of our competitive edge. Let us stop this massive financial retreat undertaken by the federal Government when it comes to post-secondary education and related matters.
Let us ask ourselves what is the financial situation regarding post-secondary education.
First, I would like to contest most strenuously the figures used by Government Members. They use figures like $6.9 billion, $7.3 billion, $20 billion, $103 billion or 23 per cent of such and such. Those Canadians who are listening to this debate simply do not have the experience of dealing with millions, let alone with billions. The suggestion has been made that there is massive support for post-secondary education, but if one looks at it in context, that is not at all an accurate description of what is occurring.
What is the financial situation regarding post-secondary education today? In 1986 $8 billion, not $8 million, was reduced from transfer payments to the provinces for health and education. In 1989, $4 billion, not $4 million, was reduced. Those are rough figures, but they are very, very close.
Quite apart from that, there has been a $700 million reduction in training and retraining. Then the Government adds another $800 million to it and tries to pretend that it has increased funding for training and retraining. It has said this without looking at increases in student enrolment, without looking at increased programs, without looking at needed new equipment or any of those variables. Quite apart from that, there are plants and equipment that are getting older and require more dollars for maintenance. That is being drawn from general revenues.
The Government neglects to point out that there has been a 30 per cent increase in enrolment in universities in the last decade. In that decade, there has been an increase of only 8 per cent in the teaching workforce at those universities. It neglects to mention that professors need to deal with large, overloaded classes and it is becoming increasingly difficult for educators to give the kind of education to which our youth are entitled.
Let us look for a moment at student aid. The cost of living criteria has not been changed since 1984. Because of increases in salaries, that means that the student must pay a greater proportion toward his education. Those parents who support their children who are going to post-secondary educational institutions are also paying more.
June 20, 1989

Current levels of funding have in fact been frozen. The program for an increasing part-time student population has been a disaster, and that has been acknowledged by all Parties. In this Budget, current overall levels for student aid have been frozen.
Let us look at research and development. One half of our Gross Domestic Product is devoted to research and development. That is one half of that which is devoted to it by our major competitor, the United States, and it is roughly one half of what is contributed to it by Japan, Sweden and a number of countries that are smaller than Canada and overall have fewer riches than Canada does.
We have not even looked at the hidden costs, and there are many. One example is postal subsidies. It would appear as if postal subsidies available to learned journals and scholarly books will no longer be available. This will be an additional financial burden on those institutions and on the educational system in general.
This massive retreat will increase regional disparities. The poor will have to pay more, and by the poor, I mean the citizens and the poorer provinces. There will be fewer graduates from those areas of Canada that are poor and therefore regional disparities will increase.
I would argue that it is quite appropriate to target funds after consultation with the provinces. I am sure that there can be some accommodation made, but we need to come through with the funds in order to support that infrastructure that will either make us competitive or not competitive, not only with the United States but on the world scene.
Spending on education, training, retraining and research and development needs to be looked upon not only as an expenditure but as an investment. If Hon. Members doubt what I say, they should look at the number of investments made by the United States, Japan and a number of other countries in the area of education, training, retraining and research and development. There are such things as good debts and bad debts. A good debt is one that returns on the investment made and a bad debt, of course, is one which does not make that return. I would submit that with education, training, retraining and research and development, there is a great deal of return on the investment.
Post-Secondary Education

We are losing our competitive edge. There have been numerous cuts. What has the impact been? It has meant extra costs for provinces, students and their parents. Our young people are losing hope.
Laid-off workers, especially older ones, are driven to despair. The Canadian people are confused. They realize the deficit must be reduced, but on the other hand they question this Government's priorities. This should be a tremendous opportunity for the Government to discharge its responsibility as regards post-secondary education. Let them do so, and let them do it now! Let them give postsecondary education its due!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed the speech of the Hon. Member for Windsor- Lake St. Clair (Mr. McCurdy). I thought it was well delivered, and obviously the Hon. Member cares about the youth of Canada. It needs to be said, however, that all of us care about the youth of Canada. All of us want to find the right combination of actions which will end up securing a very promising future for those young people. It is in that spirit of caring about what comes next, of caring about the next generation, that the federal Budget was framed. I really believe that. The Hon. Member talked about the burden of the deficit, and that economic imperatives should not outweigh social imperatives. That is an interesting concept. I agree with the Hon. Member that in a perfect world we should invest whatever needs to be invested for research and development and education. As the Hon. Member well knows, we are not living in a perfect world.
I would like to make a couple of comments on the motion the Hon. Member has put before the House. When the Government came to office in 1984, it was quickly realized that we had a serious debt problem. The Government has been on a course of action since then to attempt to get the debt problem under control. There has been some success. The debt has been reduced from 24 per cent in 1984 to less than 10 per cent now. Is that good enough? No, not by any means is it good enough. Still Canada faces a serious problem in the future. The Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in April accelerated us on the road to being more responsible in terms of debt control and management.

June 20, 1989
Post-Secondary Education
The Hon. Member for Windsor-Lake St. Clair (Mr. McCurdy) would have to agree that the key point in maintaining our social programs is maintaining our ability to fund them. That is pivotal. We can talk in the House about how we are not spending enough in different areas, programs, agencies, on education and on R and D. However, unless we have the facility as a country to make good on those promises, what is said here contains empty words. We need to be more realistic about what we can and cannot do.
The debt that Canada has accumulated and the debt service costs which make that debt rise on a daily basis threaten our economic ability to sustain prosperity. The Hon. Member has to agree with that. We are spending $30 billion a year on debt service payments. Imagine what $30 billion a year could do to funding education. It would be wonderful to be relieved of the burden of financing this debt, but we are not.
What steps can the Government responsibly and realistically take to get the debt monkey off our backs, and at the same time tiy and maintain a caring and human face to the Government? I submit to the Hon. Member that we are attempting to find that formula. It is important to remember that we are not looking at absolute cuts in funding here. The Member's motion is flawed in its wording, because it talks about restoring funds cut from federal transfer payments. That is not exactly true.
Transfer payments to other levels of Government from the federal Government amount to 24 per cent of government spending. That is a significant amount of money. In absolute dollars it is $34 billion which is transferred from Ottawa to the provinces. If the Government wants to become more responsible about how it is spending its money, it cannot ignore those transfer payments; it cannot ignore a budgetary item so large. Therefore, the Government is correct in looking at this.
Established Programs Financing contributions amount to almost $20 billion in 1989-90. The next largest federal transfer program is equalization at $7 billion, and the Canada Assistance Plan at $5 billion. On a per capita basis, that represents $750 for every single Canadian in this year. Therefore, it is a significant amount of money.
Of course, federal assistance through EPF helps the provinces, as the Hon. Member has stated, meet their responsibilities for health and post-secondary education. EPF also forms the largest part of federal support for health and post-secondary education. Federal transfers under EPF arrangements are indexed to grow annually, and they take the form of a block fund. Federal assistance is not linked to how much provinces spend in a particular area.
The 1989 Budget announced that the growth rate of those transfer payments will be reduced by 1 per cent. That is not a cut. There will continue to be a rate of growth and the funds will continue to grow and get larger year after year. Therefore, there has not been a cut in transfer payments to the provinces. Over the next five years EPF is expected to total nearly $108 billion. That is an increase of $24 billion. How can that possibly be a cut when it is going to increase by $24 billion? EPF transfers to the provinces will match or exceed the rate of inflation. When something is growing by $24 billion, when it is exceeding the rate of inflation and getting larger, how can it be a cut?
I might point out to the Hon. Member that for Ontario, the province that he and I are from, the hard numbers indicate that in 1989-90 the estimated EPF and equalization transfers to Ontario will be $7.2 billion. In 1991 they will be $7.6 billion. That is an increase in one year of $429 million. It is not a cut.
This year for the Province of Quebec, transfer payments will be $8.1 billion, and next year they will be $8.5 billion. That is $421 million more, which is an increase. The Province of Alberta will receive a $103 million increase year over year; British Columbia will receive a $133 million increase. Those are not cuts.
I submit that the motion before the House has been improperly drafted by stating: "the Government should restore funds cut from federal transfer payments". Those funds have not been cut.
On top of this, the equalization program provides substantial additional federal assistance to lower-income provinces to help them in providing services to the public. Equalization payments are unconditional transfers to the provinces. Provinces can also use those funds to finance important services such as education.
June 20,1989

Robust growth in overall provincial revenues, together with strong economic growth in Ontario, has substantially increased these payments. This year they are expected to exceed $7 billion.
Not only are EPF transfers continuing to grow, but so are total major transfers to provinces. In 1984-85 they were $25 billion. By 1989-90 they will have increased to $34 billion. That is an increase, a growth of $9 billion. It is not a cut.
EPF is the largest single program of assistance to post-secondary education, but it is by no means the only form of help that the federal Government gives to the provinces. There are student loan programs and granting councils.
The Liberal Member who spoke a moment ago talked about good debt and bad debt. I will concede that the Hon. Member made a good point in that there is a differentiation in the type of debt incurred. However, there is another type of debt which shackles and can destroy whole nations. Canadians need only look south to other countries that have travelled the road of excessive spending leading to mounting debt problems to see where the road ends. I remind the Hon. Member for Windsor-Lake St. Clair that this road ends in the inability of a country to fund the social programs he has defended and spoken to so eloquently.
I share his concern for the youth of this country. However, I say to the Hon. Member that we have to clean up our financial house, get it in order, get Canada back on a solvent basis, and then we can have the caring, kind, and humane face to this country that the Hon. Member and I would both like to see.

He used the term, one which I wrote down when he said it, "self-created deficit", as though it is some mysterious object that all of a sudden appeared on the scene and now we have to ignore it in order to get on with important matters like education. I want him to know that education has always been important. However, there were a few intervening actions which occurred that created this mysterious self-created deficit that we are all so concerned about now.
First, let us go back to 1972 and 1974, the period of a minority Government. David Lewis was the leader of the Party of the Hon. Member. The Liberal Party was very anxious to maintain its hold on the Government for as long as possible. Thus there was a convenient arrangement made between the governing Liberal Party and David Lewis and his operatives so that they could have a temporary coalition in order to stay in office.
During that time some things came into being, mysteriously, such as the Mackenzie Valley Pipeline Commission headed by Tom Berger. That Commission managed to stall energy operations in western Canada for a good many years. In fact, that part of it has not done well since. In fact, in terms of threats of oil spills on the West Coast of Canada, we would not have had to worry about them if they would have allowed the pipeline to be built.
Then there was a little corporation known as PetroCan created. It was bom as a result of this coalition that came into being between 1972 and 1974. PetroCan was supposed to be a window on the industry with just a small cash infusion of $500,000-an insignificant amount. However, the window went on to become a bay window. It kept getting bigger and bigger until the corporation is now monumental. It is a multi-billion dollar corporation with a glass tower in Calgary known as Red Square. This $500,000 company was begun as a result of the coalition which created this self-created deficit.
Then, Mr. Lalonde, who was the Minister at the time, bought a foreign oil company that was operating in Canada. He paid $1 billion too much for it, something which inflated the whole price of Petro-Canada. Now, a few years later, we have to think of how we are going to pay back the debt that was incurred by the loose spending of that loose coalition which seemed so innocent and so human at the time. The most human thing it could have done would have been to think about education. It was profligate in terms of its spending in those

June 20, 1989
Post-Secondary Education
days. Deficit spending was thought to be a buzzword, an in word for people who were in this coalition. It was good because it thought of the people. That deficit is now robbing 30 per cent of our income. We cannot spend it on education anymore. We cannot spend it on health services the way we would like to. The Hon. Member now sees that as a self-created deficit. The Member who was an educator wants to see us ignore the deficit.
Incidentally, as my colleague just pointed out, the Hon. Member who proposes the motion talked about cutbacks and cuts in spending. Between 1979 and 1984 Established Programs Financing hit a peak of $54,929 billion. From 1984 to 1989 the figure rose to $83,354 billion, an increase of nearly $30 billion as I read it. However, the Hon. Member calls that increase a cut. Between 1989 and 1994 it is expected that Established Programs Financing will rise to $107,865 billion. Is that a cut? That figure is double what it was between 1979 and 1984. Yet the Hon. Member persists in calling it a cut.
I know that money is important in education. Without it we cannot get into all the areas that we need to get into such as research in microbiology, space research, sound-all of the matters that universities have to get into if we are to become world leaders in these areas. However, they all cost money. Everything in education does not cost money. I wish the Hon. Member as an educator himself would have said something about the place of curiosity in education, the place of working one's way through school and giving oneself an incentive in education.

speechtext:
There are four motions on the Order Paper and Notices offered in amendment to Bill C-8, an Act to amend the Department of Labour Act, all in the name of the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. Proud).

Motion No. 2 is identical to a motion that was moved and negatived in committee. For this reason it will not be selected.
Motion No. 3 causes the Chair misgivings because the amendment is attempting to add a definition of a "Consultative Council Board". It is my view that the amendment goes beyond the scope of the Bill as read a second time by the House.
Paragraph one of Citation 773 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition stipulates that: "An amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant to the Bill, beyond its scope or governed by or dependent upon amendments already negatived".

Motion No. 1
That Bill C-8 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out lines 11 to 14
at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"ions, employees or employee organizations, for the purpose of
making provision".
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise today to speak on this motion. Specifically, the motion calls for Bill C-8 to be amended by striking out lines 11 to 14 at page 1 and substituting this motion. Clause 5(1) of Bill C-8 would now read:
Subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, the Minister may enter into agreements with provincial Governments, employers, employer organizations, employees, or employee organizations, for the purposes of making provision.
Bill C-8 is an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code, enabling the establishment of the Program for Older Worker Adjustment, otherwise known as POWA.
It has been more than three years since the Government announced its intention to create a program for older worker adjustment and, finally, the Government has brought forward legislation. It is important to note that this announcement by the Government came directly on the heels of its decision to cancel the Labour Adjustment Benefit Program in the Government's February 1986 Budget.
During the debate at second reading of Bill C-8, I addressed this matter and I want to reaffirm that my colleagues on this side of the House are very upset with the Government for taking more than three years to bring this legislation to fruition.
Given the time frame that the Government had to produce legislation that could greatly benefit older workers, what we see here is legislation that is a step in the right direction, although a minor step forward at best.

June 20, 1989
Labour
I say that because during the three years that older workers have been waiting for a new program there have been approximately and still are 636 applications involving thousands of older workers. They have been waiting a long while and my colleagues and I on this side of the House do not think that they should wait any longer. They had been promised a program by the Government; they were promised benefits and assistance.
Throughout the legislative committee hearings this theme was constantly brought forward by the witnesses. Although they felt that there were inherent flaws in this particular legislation, substantial flaws, they still felt it was important to support this legislation. A major concern was the involvement of financial institutions in the administration of this program.
The Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Labour Market Productivity Centre, and the Canadian Council on Social Development raised this concern during the hearings. That is why I am proposing this motion in the House today.
The Canadian Labour Market and the Productivity Centre suggested that a better model for administering income maintenance could be through the Canada Pension Plan and proposed that this program somehow be administered through Health and Welfare Canada. In terms of the annuity model, they proposed that instead of privatizing the delivery of this program, systems already in place could take care of the same issue.
The Canadian Council on Social Development questioned how the program administration with the financial institutions, and more specifically with insurance companies, would actually work in practice. During the legislative committee hearings the Canadian Council on Social Development stated:
We question the appropriateness of business firms making adjustments to the benefits payments, once the initial benefit level has been established by POWA. How will private firms monitor changes in annuity holders' employment and income status without reference to personal information on these annuity holders' income tax returns?
The Canadian Labour Congress had reservations about the involvement of financial institutions in the administration of this program. One concern was the transfer of work from unionized public workers to
non-unionized private sector workers. Another concern raised by the CLC was that the purchase of annuities virtually guarantees that the provision of income security to older workers will be administratively segregated from the other aspects of an integrated adjustment program, which include training, job counselling and job placement. To summarize the feelings of the CLC, I think it is safe to say that to turn over the income situation of POWA beneficiaries to financial institutions was, according to them, totally unacceptable.
Given the concerns raised by these notable organizations during the legislative committee hearings, I propose that the House consider the adoption of this motion that is before us today.
These organizations have a very strong insight into the concerns with respect to older workers in this country. The dilemmas facing older workers today, and in the past, are not new to these organizations, for they have researched this area for many years and have provided us, as parliamentarians and Canadians, with very thorough studies. I trust that this motion will receive positive consideration by the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in favour of the motion. The major reason why I do so concerns an element of privatization to a portion of the Government, and perhaps the involvement by the private sector in government at all. The concept of the delivery of the benefits of the Program for Older Worker Adjustment being delivered by private insurance institutions is one I find particularly abhorrent. The struggles I have had with insurance companies in the delivery of workers' benefits for sickness, accident and long-term disability pale in comparison to the struggles the Opposition is having with the Government. So you can quite well imagine how enormous the problems are which people are having with private insurance companies insofar as the delivery of these programs are concerned.
Can you imagine an employee on long-term disability from a plant that is designated within this program, the employees of which are entitled to receive benefits under POWA, an employee who is most likely at two-thirds of the previous salary? POWA stipulates that the benefit levels are 60 per cent of previous salaries.
June 20, 1989

Once the enterprise has been designated under this program, I would suggest that there would be an enormous amount of pressure by that insurance company to force the levels which it was previously paying out of its own pocket of 66 per cent down to the 60 per cent and foisting the cost of that worker on to the taxpayers of the country.
I do not think it is possible to view some of the problems associated with this concept in any other way. There is absolutely no reason for insurance companies to be involved in this kind of a program at all. What we see here is simply a continuation of what was begun several years ago by this Government but which has accelerated since the return of this Parliament and certainly as a consequence of this Budget; that is, the privatization of as many services which can be provided to people ostensibly by the Government as possible.
The Government claims that the reason for doing it this way is that it is cheaper. If the Government puts these things out for tender and the cost to the Government as a result is cheaper, and they have said that it will be as much as 70 per cent, the difference in cost is quite easily explained.
As the previous speaker pointed out, and as the mover of the motion pointed out, what is happening is that the people who will be implementing this program are now going to be in the private sector and will be more poorly paid than Government workers. I would suggest that the insurance companies are able to provide the cost at somewhat less than the Government, but even on that basis what the Government is really doing, as is the case in most privatization efforts, is being penny-wise and pound-poor. If the people who are providing this service were to remain within the Government, well paid workers within the Government earning decent salaries, paying income tax and spending the money in the community, the basic overall return to the Government would be just as high as if these services were not provided by private companies.
I agree with the previous speaker that what we have here is a pale beginning of something which should have become full blown long before now, something which we have waited three years for the implementation of, the pale beginnings of something which has to occur. Older workers are at a tremendous loss within our society to
Labour
find jobs for themselves. Even the services provided to them under the Labour Department are insufficient in helping them to find jobs for a variety of reasons.
For the time being, I would simply like to point out that while we will be supporting this motion and supporting the concept of POWA, it is with a great deal of concern and sorrow that we recognize that it does not go much farther.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-8 is to provide income assistance to older workers who have lost their jobs and who, because of their age, cannot find work again. In the Bill older workers are defined as those people 55 years up to and including 64 years. This proposal to provide income assistance to older workers is of course subject to conditions. I will discuss those conditions when we come to a later amendment.
Let me say that it is obvious that one of the conditions is that the older worker must have exhausted his unemployment insurance. Therefore, what we have here is a Bill which will provide income assistance to a worker over 55 who cannot find work, who no longer has unemployment insurance. He has to have some kind of income assistance until he gets old enough to get the old age pension. That is the purpose of the Bill.
The amendment to the Bill, which we are discussing now and which has been proposed by my colleague from Prince Edward Island, is to strike out that clause of the Bill which provides that income benefits to the unemployed older workers come from private financial institutions. For some reason or other, the Government has decided to finance and provide this income assistance to older workers by making agreements with private companies and with private financial institutions.
We cannot understand why. We don't finance old age pensions by some sort of an agreement with private financial institutions. We do not provide family allowances by making a contract with private insurance companies and private finance companies to make those payments to families for family allowances. As a matter of fact, I do not know of any kind of social programs where the Government makes a contract with a private, profit-making company to provide benefits to Canadians. We have in this Bill such a provision.

June 20, 1989
Labour
The witnesses before the legislative committee recommended that that is not the way to do it. They said that these benefits should be provided for and financed like other social benefits through Government agencies such as the Canada Pension Plan,old age pensions,family allowances and so on.
The Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Council on Social Development recommended that we strike out this provision that says that the benefits will be financed and provided by financial institutions. That is what my hon. colleague is doing in this amendment.
We urge Members of this House to support the amendment so that these benefits will be financed and provided for like all other social benefits and income support benefits.
It is surprising that the Government announced this program in the Budget of February, 1986, and yet it took the government members more than three years to produce this Bill. After abolishing the previous program, they finally came forth with this Bill and program for older worker adjustment. Despite the fact that we support the goal of the Bill, it is hard to understand why there are so many flaws in the Bill such as the flaw before us. I urge the House to support this amendment put forward by my hon. colleague.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to add my support to the motion tabled here before us by the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. Proud). It is a very important amendment. More and more we are seeing in our constituency offices people who have lost their jobs and specifically between the ages of 55 and 64. My hon. friend before me referred to them as the older workers. I would like to refer to them as the more senior workers. Because they have experience, they can offer a lot to the country, perhaps for another 20 years or more. Yet firms are reluctant to hire them. That is why I think this Bill is a good one. It does provide protection for such workers who find themselves unemployed. It has a traumatic psychological effect on people to find themselves unemployed after working for 20 or 25 years. That is not an easy thing to live through. It is unfortunate that it took the Government three years to bring in such a Bill.
I hope the Government is listening and will vote for the amendments which our side is introducing because their purpose is only to improve the Bill. The Government is following a trend of cutting the public service and moving toward privatization. It has brought in the free trade Bill, the effects of which we have already seen. Plants are moving to Mexico where workers work for $4 a day. This displaces workers in Canada in the age group of 55 to 64.1 know you want to get on with the debate, Mr. Speaker, and I would urge all Members of the House to support this amendment.

Hon. Jean Corbeil (Minister of LabounMr. Speaker, I would like to point out that the proposed amendment, if adopted, would eliminate a key component of the program, a component that has played a major role in all our negotiations with the provinces on their participation in this program. Adopting this amendment would require a new series of negotiations with the provinces and might mean considerable delay in providing the assistance that older workers need. Earlier, I heard the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. Proud) say there had been too many delays already, and my point is that adopting this amendment would only make the situation much worse.
As for cancelling the previous program, I can inform the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) that we have not yet terminated the previous program. In fact, it has been extended for one year, and this was a program his Government had expected to expire in 1985.
Mr. Speaker, by striking out, as proposed by the Opposition, the words "or other such persons or entities as the Minister considers appropriate", we would in fact deprive the Minister of the option of using any other legal entity in the job environment that might be useful in facilitating adjustment payments. This would mean it would take at least one or two or maybe more years to put in place the government bureaucracy required to dispense these payments, and it would also reduce the amount of money available for the workers in question.
June 20, 1989

I therefore ask, Mr. Speaker, that the House vote down this amendment.

Nay.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 76(8) the recorded division on the motion stands deferred.

Motion No. 4
That Bill C-8 be amended by adding immediately after line 14 at page 2 the following new clause:
"2. (1) Three years after the coming into force of this Act, a comprehensive review of the provisions of section 5 of the Department of Labour Act, as enacted by this Act, shall be undertaken by such committee of the House of Commons as maybe designated or established by the House for that purpose.
(2) The committee referred to in subsection (1) shall, within a year after the review is undertaken or within such further time as the House of Commons may authorize, submit a report on the review to the House including a statement of any changes the committee recommends."
He said: The last motion that I have the pleasure of speaking on today in reference to Bill C-8 is a motion proposing that the Bill be amended by adding, after line 14 on page 2, the following new clause numbered 2(1), and I quote:
Three years after the coming into force of this Act, a comprehensive review of the provisions of section 5 of the Department of Labour Act, as enacted by this Act, shall be undertaken by such committee of the House of Commons as may be designated or established by the House for that purpose.
Labour
There are a myriad of concerns with respect to this legislation, as I have addressed in previous comments to the House and throughout the legislative committee process. Obviously these concerns have been shared by my colleagues and by numerous organizations and individuals throughout the country.
As previously mentioned in this House, my colleagues and I support this Bill in principle. By that I mean that older workers need assistance and they have waited long enough for such a program.
I would briefly like to highlight some of the concerns that have been raised pertaining to the legislation. I believe that, although it is definitely an improvement to have a program for older workers' assistance, this legislation has an unusually high degree of selectivity, arbitrariness and subjectivity.
The criteria for eligibility is very broad and does not take into account older workers who may fall between the cracks so to speak. What about older workers who are not part of a major permanent lay-off as designated by the Minister? We still have no idea what the Government will consider as being a major lay-off. Will the Government judge by the number of employees laid off in a region or by the severity of an individual's situation? These lay-offs are to be assessed on a case by case basis.
Given the loosely worded criteria for deciding who qualifies, it is left totally to the discretion of the Minister of Labour as to what constitutes a major lay-off and thus who will be eligible for assistance. The motion I have proposed today will ensure that if the concerns are raised in this area strongly enough to warrant review that the House will do so.
With respect to the federal-provincial partnership of this program, the Government is saying that it will be 70-30 cost shared. It is important to note that Ontario is the only province that has not agreed to participate. British Columbia has recently entered the program. Why has Ontario not agreed to participate? We haven't been given any reasons for its reluctance. Does this mean that older workers from Ontario will not have the same rights and opportunities as older workers from the other nine provinces?
Another concern is how the program will mesh with the UI proposals. How will the design for programs for older workers under the labour force development strategy mesh with POWA? Will they be used to test eligibility for POWA? Will older workers have to exhaust all alternatives in order to qualify for the Program for Older Worker Adjustment?

June 20, 1989
Labour
During the legislative committee hearings a multitude of concerns were raised, some of which I outlined a few moments ago and some of which I will outline now. POWA continues to be a passive approach to labour adjustment for older workers. Some of the witnesses at the hearings believed that it is better to put resources into training and retraining older workers rather than only providing income supplementation. The LAB program had worker and employer representation in the decision-making group built into its administration, unlike this Bill. The program should be made more consultative by including workers and employers in its administration. Under this proposed legislation there are very low yearly benefit levels, with the maximum about $13,200 in 1989 which is about the same as Statistics Canada poverty lines.
How would a lay-off be judged eligible? According to the legislation it must be a major permanent lay-off, but it could be refused if considered a minor permanent lay-off.
As we can all see, there are a variety of concerns with respect to this legislation. Thus I believe that the motion I have proposed today will ensure that these concerns will be dealt with and that other concerns that may arise will be dealt with in an effective manner. I urge the House today to support this motion which I have put forward.

Mr. Speaker, there are several very good reasons for supporting this motion, not the least of which is that there is a lack of regulatory authority within Bill C-8 itself. That highlights more than ever the necessity for a review. I cannot think of a better vehicle for reviewing this legislation than the House itself and a committee set up by it.
It needs a review process because all it says really is that the Minister will enter into negotiations. There is not any major evaluation of what the final program will look like. All we really have at this stage before it becomes law is reference to some Department of Labour documents which are not very extensive in their exposition of what the program will entail.
The motion will also provide a public review of the program for older workers. Related to what I have already said, this program contains the vaguest of references and operates largely upon the goodwill of the Government. In light of what we are experiencing in relation to this Government at the present time, how can we have any assurance that the designations of major lay-offs are going to be fair? It is absolutely essential that the public have some input. It might possibly be that three years is too long a period of time. It is absolutely essential that the public have some ability to be able to review this program after it has had a chance to operate for a while.
The third reason that it is essential that we have the review is that when it comes to older workers, they face many problems within society as a result of losing their employment which other age levels do not experience. Not the least of which, Mr. Speaker, is the inability to be able to find work at the age of 55 to 64. It is almost a given within our society that people of this age are going to have difficulty finding employment.
In addition, a review of this very situation is going to be essential because the older worker, the 55 to 64 year-old age group, while they are becoming a larger portion of Canadian society are becoming a smaller proportion of the labour force, indicating something in reverse to what one would hope to see happen.
Since that is the case, with a review three years from now we will be able to take a look at where this trend is leading us and be able to make a very good assessment as to whether or not programs should be put in place to supplement this one and the degree to which this one should be augmented if that should be the indication.
I can only say in relation to the whole program for older workers that it is a pale semblance of what we ought to be having. It is a beginning. Let us hope that it is the beginning of a program which takes care of not only these people from 55 to 64 years of age who find themselves at odds with their society because they are unable to find work, but also there are developing serious problems of people even at lower ages. A review three years from now may also include the problems of workers who are even younger than 55.
June 20, 1989

Mr. Speaker, as my hon. colleague said, the purpose of this amendment is to require a review of the legislation after three years. That amendment was proposed to us by witnesses before the legislative committee. The reason that they proposed this review after three years is because they wanted the Bill to go through now, but they said it was subject to many flaws. They felt that the flaws should be dealt with in due course.
For example, the Bill contains no appeal procedure. In the former legislation, the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program, there was an appeal process which workers or firms could use if they felt the administration had not treated them properly. There is no appeal procedure in this. There is no consultation procedure written into the program.
The Minister has almost total discretion under this Bill. He can do pretty much as he likes. Many of the individuals who spoke to us felt there should be a consultation process whereby the Minister would have to consult with labour and with management with respect to this whole process for older workers.
Another flaw is that the benefits payable under this legislation are higher than welfare but lower than unemployment insurance. It is somewhere between unemployment insurance benefits and welfare benefits. This means that while it will be better to receive assistance under this Bill than under provincial welfare schemes, it will be less than some people would receive under unemployment insurance. There are flaws in the Bill. As a matter of fact, there is very little in the Bill. The Bill is only two pages. Most of the program that relates to the administration of the Bill, the criteria and so on, are in directives which are internal in the Department. We have the directives and we are able to read them but they are not in the Bill. This is another flaw.
The Government itself has put a similar provision in other legislation which is brought before Parliament. This Conservative Government has used that type of clause before, that legislation should be reviewed after three years or after five years. When we were in power, we did it with the Freedom of Information legislation and the Privacy legislation. We did it at that time at the request of the Conservative Party. They had proposed it in the House, such as we are doing tonight and we
Labour
agreed to it. That legislation was subject to review. A parliamentary committee studied it and made a report on improvements.
I would urge the Minister of Labour to take this proposed amendment seriously. It does not change the legislation as such now, but it will require that the legislation be reviewed in three years' time by a designated parliamentary committee. The parliamentary committee can propose improvements to the law at that time on the basis of three years' experience. I have already mentioned some of the flaws in the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I too support in principle the amendment that is proposed, which basically renders this legislation reviewable after three years. It seems to me that it is a good move to review the purpose and effect of this particular legislation and the impact it has in Canada generally.
Having said that, I would like to indicate my very serious concerns with respect to the fundamental problem that Bill C-8 purports to address. That fundamental problem, Mr. Speaker, is one that you, I and every Member of the House of Commons encounters almost on a daily basis in our constituencies. That is the older workers who find themselves unemployed through no reason of their own.
We know all too often major plants and minor employers for economic reasons, whether it is because of free trade or because of other economic considerations, decide to close their plants. The closure of a plant or the closure of a place of employment has brutal effects on workers, especially those workers who are older. This particular Bill deals with workers who are between the ages of 55 and 65.
Regardless of what age one may be, the impact of losing a job is very severe and especially when the person losing his or her job is the major breadwinner in the family. Having said that, the problem is even more acute when we are dealing with older workers. As their Member of Parliament, I have older workers calling me in desperation looking for some type of employment. They find themselves somewhat short of 60 years of age when they would qualify for a reduced Canada Pension Plan, or several years away from Old Age Security. The impact is devastating on a family where at one moment there is an income and the next moment there is not.

June 20, 1989
Labour
Bill C-8 tries to address that particular problem and although the Bill ought to be supported, especially in view of the great number of applicants-I understand there are 636 applicant groups that apply for benefits under this legislation-but this is not the answer. It is simply ad hoc, it is piecemeal and it is also discriminatory. If you are 54 years of age, you do not qualify. What is the difference between a 54 year old worker with three or four children, a mortgage to pay and other expenses to meet and a 55 year old worker with four children, a mortgage to pay and expenses to meet? What is the difference between the two when they lose their jobs? There isn't any.
Unfortunately the Government has arbitrarily chosen age 55 as being the operative age after which benefits may be payable under this legislation. That is a fundamental flaw in the legislation in that it only applies to older workers beyond the age of 55.
What the Government of Canada ought to be looking at is not an amendment to the Department of Labour Act, Bill C-8-here it is 8.20 p.m., a few weeks before we are adjourning to fulfil a commitment made by the Government in 1986-but it ought to be addressing the fundamental problem in a serious and comprehensive way. What I am speaking of is a form of guaranteed annual income or an income supplement program available to all Canadians. There comes a time when we have to talk about the ultimate social program. In Canada today we have a myriad of programs, whether it is at the provincial, municipal or federal level. There are welfare programs, unemployment insurance, Canada Pension Plan, mothers' allowance, all kinds of ways in which the Government tries to assist those in need. At some point in the future the Government will have to realize that each and every Canadian, regardless of where he or she lives, regardless of being male or female, whether he or she is 65 years or 25 years of age, people are all entitled to a certain minimum standard of living. That is the least we can do as a modem, prosperous and civilized nation.
I see that not only my colleagues in the Liberal Party are supportive of a comprehensive review of all welfare systems in Canada-the beginning of a discussion of a guaranteed annual income program in Canada-but I note the Minister himself and other Ministers of the Crown nodding in agreement. Indeed, various backbenchers agree as well. I would hope that all those who
agree will urge the Minister, the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to give serious consideration to addressing the root problem that this Bill purports to address.
I note that I am permitted to speak on the motion and I understand that third reading will follow when my beloved colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), the deputy whip, will speak. Not so long ago he was not a member of management. Now he is and he is telling me to speed up. I will conclude by saying-
Hear, hear!
I see there is considerable support for me to continue.
Oh, oh!
My colleagues are so appreciative of my submissions.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to be brief. Let me say that the Hon. Member who just spoke and I do not have the same understanding of the applause that went on while he was speaking. I gather it was more an encouragement to put an end to his speech than to what he was saying.
Oh, oh!

I think that this Bill is a tribute to both my predecessors, the Hon. Member from Vaudreuil, the Hon. Member from Kindersley-Lloydminster and the officers of the Department of Labour, who have put together a new program that is a monument of flexibility that will fill the need that is so important for the older worker.
The program is flexible and will also provide the necessary help for older workers. This is a joint federal-provincial program and it would be in keeping with the consultative nature of this program to review activities with the provinces. Moreover, Members of Parliament have the opportunity annually to examine the activities under the Department of Labour Act through their annual review of Labour Canada's Estimates. Also, a committee has been put together consisting of representatives from the provincial Governments, the federal Government, labour and employers to make sure the program fits the needs for which it was designed.
June 20,1989

Mr. Speaker, in my share of time this evening on these two motions and on the motions I put forward I want to say that this Bill is going to pass. We have said throughout the hearings that people have been waiting for this legislation. We are not totally satisfied and as my colleagues have said, there are other ways to look more in depth at these social
Labour
programs. I hope that many of our concerns about who will qualify, about what is a major lay-off, concerns I have put forward today, in committee and at second reading stage, will be addressed. I look forward to seeing the results of this Bill as it becomes law.

Mr. Speaker, during the debate in the House over the last three or four days, I have kept hearing references to the Budget made by government Members. Government Members are claiming that a great deal less is really a lot more, but that in the odd case where there is more government control it is really less.
In the final analysis the program for older workers is the same. In 1985 under the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program, which I grant did not have as wide an application as POWA, more people were covered. They were covered at higher levels and they received more money.
There is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 73,000 people who are in the age group of 55 to 64. The Program for Older Workers, under the best of circumstances, cannot cover more than 10 per cent of those people who may be potentially affected by becoming unemployed at that age. That is one of our major concerns. What will happen to that 90 per cent of people who will potentially find themselves out of work with no possibility whatsoever of being able to avail themselves of the Program for Older Workers?
It is true that the sooner this Bill gets passed, the better, but it is also true that there are many older workers who anticipate benefiting from this program who will not. They will not benefit from it because they will find themselves in what is identifiably a major lay-off which, under the terms of this program, terms that are certainly vague enough, will not be a lay-off that is deemed to be severe enough. Therefore, they will be excluded from receiving the benefits of this program.
This Bill will be implemented. We in the New Democratic Party will not vote against it. However, we would ask government Members to look at it again. I cannot for the life of me understand why they would object to having this program reviewed after three years. If it will be as good as they say it will be, I would think that they would welcome the initiative of the Hon. Member from Prince Edward Island who moved the motion that there be a review after three years.
June 20, 1989

Labour
The legislation is fraught with many problems. It does not go far enough. However, some people will be helped, though not enough. Let us help those who need the help.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, this amendment would provide some very necessary and useful assistance for older workers who have lost their jobs as a result of major and permanent lay-offs and have no prospects of re-entering the labour market. These workers are some of the most deserving people in this country.

In third reading stage of this Bill I would like to thank the members of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party for the constructive perspectives they offered during the hearings of the legislative committee and for their co-operation in ensuring the speedy passage of this brief legislative amendment to the Department of Labour Act.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I wish to make one or two other points with respect to Bill C-8, a Bill which purports to address the problem of unemployed older workers.
First, the Bill does not go far enough. It is somewhat discriminatory in that it applies to a certain group of older workers, those between the ages of 55 and 65. I hope the Minister has sought and received the advice of law officers of the Crown to determine whether this legislation complies with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As the Minister knows, under Section 15 of the Charter, it is prohibited to discriminate based on age.
As I indicated earlier, this Bill does discriminate. It discriminates in a positive way in that it provides benefits to a certain group of people. However, it discriminates in a negative way against those who are not between the ages of 55 and 65.
People who are 54 years of age will be discriminated against by this legislation. In my respectful submission, the Bill is contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. However, the Minister nodded when I asked him if he received the advice of lawyers on that point.
A general point has been made by a number of my colleagues on several occasions with respect to the arbitrary age at which the Government of Canada tells workers that they must retire or become eligible for benefits. I am speaking of two programs in particular. Under the Canada Pension Plan, people become eligible for reduced pensions at the age of 60 and they become eligible for full pensions at the age of 65. With respect to the Old Age Security Program, a program which up until recently was open to all Canadians but for which the Government has now introduced a claw-back, workers who turn 65 years of age become eligible.
There is nothing magical about turning 60 years of age or 65 years of age. At some point in the past a Government in its wisdom decided that that was the age when people had to consider themselves old, when it was time to be removed from the workforce. I would ask that parliamentarians, particularly the Minister and government Members, give serious thought to those arbitrary ages which were selected for the Old Age Security and the Canada Pension Plan.
The age of 65 is not a magical age. There are workers who are 55 and wish to retire for health reasons or other reasons. Surely, in a modem, prosperous, affluent country like Canada, we can find the resources to permit older workers who wish to retire the opportunity to do so with a pension from the Government of Canada, keeping in mind, of course, that when an older worker removes himself or herself from the workforce, whether voluntarily or involuntarily, a position opens up for another worker. Those are the other two points I wish to make for the record, Mr. Speaker, and I thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak.
