speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express to the members of the Standing Committee on Transport my appreciation of their excellent spirit of co-operation in the study of the Bill. As I look around at the audience tonight, I see several members of the Transport Committee present. On behalf of the Minister, I wish to thank them for their co-operation.
Political partisanship was set aside, and a real spirit of co-operation was demonstrated by all. I wish to thank all members of the Standing Committee for that.
The key point is that the Bill which emerged is much better legislation. Co-operation in the pursuit of improvements has shown its value in the end product. For this, members of the Standing Committee can be justifiably proud.
Obviously we did not in the end satisfy everyone completely. I do not believe that this is ever possible, and some ideas for changes to the Bill could not work without totally changing the concept of the proposed Bill.
I am reminded of one definition of a camel: a camel is a horse designed by a committee. The members of the Standing Committee avoided that pitfall. Instead, they took a reasonably good work horse and made it into something closer to a thoroughbred.
Among the amendments to the Bill, the addition of oil and gas pipelines to the board's jurisdiction deserves mention. Those pipelines were not initially included in
Accident Investigation
the Bill, because they have not traditionally fallen within the scope of transportation, the subject of this Bill.
Members of the Standing Committee noted, however, that there exists a perceived potential for conflict of interest when the regulators of oil and gas pipelines are also the accident investigators. It is therefore only logical that accidents involving oil and gas pipelines, as well as pipelines carrying other commodities, be investigated by an independent board.
The object of the board was also expanded by amendments. The Bill now provides that the board may pursue its over-all objective of improving transportation safety by conducting special studies and investigations on matters pertaining to transportation safety.
In line with this, the board's objective of improving transportation safety was reinforced by adding the word "safety" to its title. It will be known officially as the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board.
The Government has agreed with these changes. However, I would like to add one point of clarification. The board is responsible for conducting accident investigations and studies, and it is accountable for the quality of its recommendations to improve transportation safety.
The responsibility for the safety of the transportation system itself rests with the Minister of Transport. The Minister is accountable to Parliament and to the people of Canada for transportation safety. I know that the new board, in its operation, will understand and respect the role and responsibilities of the Minister, as I know the Minister will understand and respect the role of the board.
Witnesses before the committee expressed a number of concerns that were dealt with by amendment. Many interested parties that would be affected by the board's work, for example the railway companies, sought assurances that they would be consulted on the regulations and policies of the board.
The Bill was amended to confirm that regulations will be pre-published for 90 days in The Canada Gazette. Another amendment requires the board to make public its policies regarding which accidents to investigate and how to conduct investigations. This guarantees that any interested party can have easy access to these policies and comment on them.

June 20, 1989
Accident Investigation
I expect that the board will consult with interested parties on the development of those policies in any event. Consultations will ensure that the policies are fair, reasonable, and workable. Consultation also recognizes the interest and responsibility for transportation safety shared by interested parties, especially carriers and their employees.
Representatives of the rail and marine industries also expressed some concern that the investigators' power to quarantine an accident site would unduly interrupt essential transportation services. The first and foremost priority of the board must be to find out what caused the accident in order to improve safety in the future. Without compromising this principle, it is possible for the investigators to have regard to the other objectives of the national transportation policy, namely, efficient and effective operation. The Bill was therefore amended to instruct the investigators to have regard to the desirability of minimizing the disruption to transportation service.
Thus, essential transportation services will be resumed as soon as practicable after an accident, for example, by replacing damaged rails so that trains may again pass through the accident site or by allowing a ship to continue its voyage as soon as possible.
Representatives of labour asked that the privilege accorded to air traffic control recordings be extended to include traffic control recordings in the rail and marine modes of transportation. All members of the Standing Committee agreed, and the appropriate amendment was made.
These amendments and a number of others adopted by the standing committee have improved Bill C-2. The Bill represents a major step toward maintaining the safety of our transportation system. It is the final piece in a series of safety related legislative initiatives in the past several years.
I would therefore like to reiterate my appreciation for the co-operative spirit shown by Members from all sides of this House in studying and debating the provisions of the Bill. I hope that they will now support it on third reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I concur with what the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary just said and my friend and colleague who is the Chairman on the Standing Committee on Transport just said. It was very enjoyable working through the process of this legislation. It was made enjoyable because of the people who showed such dedication in preparing themselves for the committee meetings. I thank them very much for the co-operation that they showed to the Members on this side of the House.
Having said that, there are some issues to which we still take exception. I will very briefly touch on those tonight. In our judgment we feel that the amendments which we proposed to this legislation should have been entertained with perhaps a little more seriousness. We wish even today, as the Bill is in its final stages in the House, that these amendments would have formed part of the legislation.
June 20, 1989

I might add that the proof of that will come to light to those of us who sometimes practise law when we go to our law libraries at different times and pick up statute citators on this particular legislation. We will look at the legislation and see those areas of the Bill that may have been adjudicated by the courts in this land for interpretation. In summarizing those issues time will tell whether the legislation is in fact operative or whether we should have spent more time on it.
It is interesting to note that this Bill was introduced and read the first time on April 7. It was then debated at second reading stage on April 17 and April 18 and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport on April 18.
After hearing from 45 witnesses the committee reported the Bill to the House, with amendments, on June 8. As I mentioned, we heard from over 45 witnesses, most of whom had many valuable comments, observations, and suggested amendments to contribute to the committee's analysis of the Bill. Yet, despite this wealth of evidence, we were unable to weigh it effectively. We were not able to discern which witnesses presented the most salient, cogent and prudent evidence or the best recommendations.
Within 24 hours of hearing the final witnesses the committee began its clause by clause consideration of the Bill. It was not possible to reflect on the evidence presented and assess which witnesses on balance presented the strongest evidence. Instead, we had to give a cursory review of statements and proposed amendments.
One would have thought that given the importance and implications of this Bill that the Government would have realized and appreciated the merits of giving this legislation more thoughtful consideration, something which could only have been achieved with less stringent time constraints. If the Government were adamant about having this legislation passed before June 30, why was the House convened on April 3? Moreover, why was the Government so intent on passing this legislation before June 30?
Accident Investigation
As you know full well, Mr. Speaker, Justice Estey is currently conducting a judicial review based on the Gander incident looking only at the four comers of the evidence. Does it not make good sense to postpone the passage of this Bill until the Minister receives a report and the Standing Committee on Transport is given the opportunity to examine the findings and the recommendations, if any, stemming from it?
Let us not be fooled, the Gander crash was most instrumental in prompting the drafting of Bill C-142 which died on the Order Paper in the last session of Parliament and which now forms Bill C-2, the legislation presently before us.
Granted, we are creating a multi-modal board which, along with aviation, will be responsible for investigating rail, marine, and commodity pipeline accidents. However, if it were not for the differing opinions and personality conflicts which made the Canadian Aviation Safety Board inoperative following the Gander crash, I doubt that the Government would have proceeded with such urgency to create this multi-modal board.
In essence, this legislation permits the Government to put an end to the dissension and conflicts which were making the Canadian Aviation Safety Board inoperative and drew greater attention to the controversies surrounding the Board than those surrounding the Gander crash.
Replacing the Canadian Aviation Safety Board with this legislation effectively permits the Government to get rid of those persons who were trying to bring the public's attention to some of the irregularities in aviation accident investigation in Canada.
In fact, these individuals have already received their notice. Would it not make good sense to wait to see if the Estey review sheds any light on why so much dissension surrounded the accident investigation assessment process? We can learn from this, correct our mistakes, and not allow them to happen again.
Many have said that it was personality conflicts which prompted the dissension. How many Canadians do you know, Mr. Speaker, who would be willing to put a $80,000 a year job on the line simply because they did not like someone else? These individuals did what they did as a matter of principle. I compliment those who were the dissenters on the Gander crash. They saw irregularities. They reported them, and now they are being silenced.

June 20, 1989
Accident Investigation
If there indeed were irregularities with the investigation of the Gander crash, then this legislation should not proceed. We will not know this until Mr. Justice Estey submits his report which is anticipated in another two weeks. Only then will we be in the position to proceed with the legislation that holds so much importance for accident investigation in our country.
Based on the evidence submitted to it, the committee concluded that the problem area lies more in the realm of the structure and the methodology of accident investigation rather than the number of board members or the powers of the chairman, although the latter are significant. Difficulties with the Gander crash point to problems with how the accident was investigated and how those investigators brought their findings and conclusions to the Canadian Aviation Safety Board for the consideration of the board members and the board panel.
Yet, in dealing with the legislation before us today, there was never an opportunity to examine the regulations of accident investigation. These, I would pose, were the root of most of the difficulties incurred by the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, not personality conflicts. If it were simply a matter of problems with the personnel, replacing them would have resolved any difficulties. While they are being replaced by the current legislation there is no guarantee that the same problems will not be revisited by this new legislation that will be passed because the regulations dictating the investigative assessment process have not been examined.
On May 261 attended the non-evidentiaiy hearings of the Dryden crash inquiry in Toronto. Justice Moshansky was appointed commissioner on that investigation. He will be examining as part of the scope of his authority the structure and methodology of accident investigation in Canada, along with determining the cause of the Dryden crash.
As I mentioned earlier, given the importance of such an examination, our Party moved an amendment to Clause 63, which was approved in committee, which will see that this legislation, that which is before us today, will undergo a comprehensive review in January 1993. I am pleased to say that this will allow whatever findings and recommendations which come out of the Dryden inquiry to be considered as they relate specifically to the
legislation before us. I would also assume from that amendment that we will be able at that time to look at the recommendations, if any, from the Estey inquiry, and any recommendations which should come out of that inquiry will also be incorporated into the legislation.
I am disappointed in certain areas of this legislation. We proposed a number of recommendations and amendments that we thought were substantial, including the number of members on the board that would make up the multi-modal board. We are still convinced that one of the real problems on the previous board, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, was the lack of delineation between the powers of the chairman and the powers of the board.
Try as much as we did in this new legislation to delineate the powers of the chairman and the powers of the board, we were unsuccessful in doing so. The question of confidentiality presented us with some problems. We discussed confidentiality in the previous legislation dealing with the Department of Labour Act amendment.
We have great respect for the institution of the collective agreement. We on this side of the House were concerned that the collective agreement was being used in the investigative process. We believe that the confidential statements made between the employer and the employee should remain confidential. If the investigators want any other source of information, they should take their own course rather than rely on those statements given pursuant to a particular clause in the collective agreement. It is our view that the sanctity of the collective agreement in our society should not be touched, for whatever reason or purpose.
We found it difficult to accept another clause. It concerned the acceptability of evidence after it was presented. According to the processes that are outlined and still in this section of the Act, it appears that the reverse onus is one that my colleagues on this side of the House feel even today would not stand the test of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. That causes us some concern because, as my colleague stated earlier in the debate, we all try for the benefit of all Canadians to bring in the most operative piece of legislation to look into the investigation process within our country.
June 20,1989

With those remarks, I am sure my colleague is happy that I will not go into any more detail. We compliment all members of the committee who worked on this legislation. It was an interesting process. Time will tell whether we were successful in the committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in third reading of Bill C-2, an Act to establish the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board. Like the chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport, the Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), my experience as what turns out to be one of the most senior members of the Transport Committee leads me to believe that this was a very good start for the work of the Transport Committee. We had a Bill that was non-partisan in nature. We all agreed with the intent of the Bill to provide a mechanism to investigate accidents in transportation modes.
There were some disagreements, not just between caucuses but within caucuses in terms of the final substance of that Bill. We must recognize that part of the reason we were able to do that was because of the spirit in which the Government, particularly the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Martin) and the Parliamentary Secretary came to the committee ready to listen and learn. They were not locked into the existing wording of the Bill.
As with many other Bills, we all like to think that we are planting seeds by asking specific questions and raising particular points. First, we hope we are indicating an interest, and second, hopefully, we are trying to pull from the witnesses the ammunition necessary to make changes that are appropriate to the legislation.
Accident Investigation
Of the total amendments that were moved and accepted, 19 of those were authored by Government Members. One amendment authored by a Government Member failed, and I will deal with that later. However, it was an indication that the Government was prepared to listen, at least in those areas.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Comuzzi) that there were areas in which the Government did not listen, even when it was clear some of its own Members supported a point of view different from that of the Government.
We attempted to make some changes and we lost a particular vote on a tie. I hoped the Government would return with a recommendation at this point to make the change dealing with the size of the board, but that did not happen. That is unfortunate. Time will tell whether this will be an appropriate number for the board.
I want to deal now with some of the specifics of the Bill. I spent a lot of time dealing with the issue, both as it related to the Bill and as transportation critic for my caucus. I am pleased that my colleague from Alberta, our energy critic, is in the House because one of the key changes we made was to ensure the purity of the legislation.
The basis of the legislation was that we separate the people who regulate a transportation mode from the people who investigate any accidents. Initially, Bill C-2 included an exemption for pipelines covered under the National Energy Board Act. We began to wonder why and considered that to be very inconsistent with the spirit of the legislation. We moved to change that, and an amendment I put forward was accepted by the committee, in effect by the Government, because it did not in any way attempt to block that change. That is a very important decision that was made not by the Government but by a committee of this Parliament.
The second major change, which deals less directly with the Bill than with all of Parliament, was an amendment I moved that changed the Bill in 22 different places. It is the first time in Canadian law that this has occurred. It is the first time in British Commonwealth law that instead of a chairman of the board we now have a chairperson.
It is to the credit of the Transport Committee which decided to accept that recommendation. I encourage all other committees, as they deal with legislation, to establish or amend boards to change the terminology to reflect the reality of the 1980s and 1990s.

June 20, 1989
Accident Investigation
Mr. Speaker, let me go through a couple of the other changes that were made because they are important. No longer does the new Board report to the Minister of Transport. Part of the problem that we found within the Canadian Aviation Safety Board was the perception of conflict of interest. After a lot of thought and bouncing around of ideas as to whether it should be the Minister of Justice, the Speaker of the House of Commons or the President of the Queen's Privy Council, the committee opted to send it to an individual, a Minister who does not have any hands-on responsibility for the operation of transportation, but who is a Member of Cabinet and who can fight for the Board on behalf of the Board for necessary funds in person-years to allow them to do their job. But more importantly, it separates transport from the Investigation Board. That is extremely important because the public has to feel confident that the Board will tell it like it is as opposed to trying to water it down or hide it away; very clearly a separation of powers.
The other change, and this is one of those other examples where there were differences of opinion on the committee, and in fact my colleague and good friend, the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin) and I disagreed on this particular one. That was over the name of the agency. It is now called the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board. We did not fight about it, but I voted against it because as the Parliamentary Assistant stated very clearly, it is the Minister of Transport and the Department of Transport that is responsible for safety in this country, safety of air, rail, marine and pipelines.
By putting the term safety into the Accident Investigation Board, we may in fact be misleading the people of Canada to think that this agency is the one responsible for it. It will have the responsibility for investigating accidents and making recommendations to the Minister of Transport, and anybody else for that matter, but it is up to those other bodies to make the decision as to whether those changes will be made. Ultimately, the responsibility is with the Government. We differed on that, but so be it. That was the nature of the debate that we had in committee where Members of the Government caucus differed from time to time. I cannot remember whether any Members of the Liberal caucus
split on any particular motions, but certainly the option was there. It was very appropriate that we approach it that way.
One of the other areas that we worked on, and it goes back to part of the problem with the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, and that was the personality conflict. There were members of that Board who did not see eye to eye but who were all appointed by the Government of the day, but with no public process, no mechanism to say to the aviation industry that it would have two people on the Board and asking who it would it like to propose. The same thing for marine and for rail. My colleague and I put forward a motion. If it had been accepted, it would have provided for the establishment of a selection committee for each mode. Then we would get people who had the confidence of the transportation areas they would be investigating.
I alluded to this earlier. We wanted to change the number of members on the Board from five to seven because we thought that unfortunately there was more than enough work in Canada to investigate all of these modes of travel and that seven people would be more appropriate. It was lost on a tie vote with the chairman voting for the status quo as is his responsibility. We also attempted to put in place some temporary members so that from time to time, when the workload became too heavy, the Minister could pull in some additional people for the Board to help out.
We also made a number of other changes throughout the Bill, but in a couple of key areas there was a lot of concern expressed. Again, it was over the conflict within CASB in terms of who was to give the chairperson of the Board the power. Should it come directly by legislation or should it be passed on from the Board itself to the chairman? In other words, the five-member Board collectively would decide what the powers of the chairperson would be. The Government Members opted to maintain the existing structure, which is that through legislation the powers are given to the Chair. The reason that we wanted to make it a conscious decision is that if there are problems in the future with a new Board, if we do get fundamental splits, that at the very least we know that the Government of the day had a chance to change it so the power was collective rather than singular, and they would have to accept the responsibility.
June 20, 1989

The other thing that we tried to do in that same mode was to make sure that the directors of investigation were appointed by the Board rather than the chairperson. Again, we think it is part of the ownership that the Board has to feel good about the decisions and the investigation that is being conducted on their behalf.
Another amendment was to change the reporting system so that the reports would come directly to Parliament rather than going through the Minister and without the necessity for the Minister to have time to respond. A number of other amendments were put forward. We had a lot of discussion and by no means was there a consistent view in terms of whether or not there should be draft reports.
For those of you who are not aware of what the Act says, it provides that a draft report from the Board shall go to Ministers and to interested parties. They have a period of time in which they can respond and point out technical errors. It does not include the recommendations. A number of people argued that there could again be the perception of conflict of interest by allowing the Minister of Transport or a pilots' association or an aircraft company to come back to the Board and get them to change the report. Therefore, we tried at first to delete that reference so that the Board would create a final report and it would become public. That failed. So then we attempted to, at the very least, have appended to the report a list of the changes that were made and why they were made and who they were requested by or, if they were not changed, the fact that they were requested. Everything was above board once again with people feeling confident in what the Board was doing.
In addition to the draft report, there is an interim report that can be requested by any Minister responsible for a department having a direct interest in the subject matter of the investigation; primarily the Minister of Transport, but it could be the Minister of National Defence. Perhaps it could even be the Minister of the Environment. But they can request an interim report when they feel it is warranted because of lapse of time and they know the investigation has gone to a certain point. We wanted to make sure that any observers would also have the opportunity to get that report. It was decided that that did not make sense.
Accident Investigation
The other thing we wanted to do was to build in an appeal mechanism for when the Board came down with its report, with its recommendations.If a particular group feels that it is not sufficient, or they are not happy with the work that was done-perhaps as was suggested with Gander that they did not look at certain things-currently there is no way formally that they can request the matter to be re-opened. The Board, in its own wisdom, if it gets new evidence, can re-open it, but what we had proposed was a recommendation that they could get in touch with the Minister who in turn would automatically request the Board to re-examine it. So there would be at least a mechanism for their participation once again, just so there would be no way that it could be left hanging.
One of the key amendments that was accepted-in fact the final version was a draft put forward by the Government-was to ensure that communications in all modes of traffic would be treated the same. Initially, the Bill dealt with air traffic control or the air mode, but it was not as concise in terms of rail and marine. So we have changed the Bill to ensure that any communications, whether from the cab of a locomotive or from a vessel to the Coast Guard, are protected under this Act.
One of the unusual things that we did in terms of the railway mode was that we had both the railway companies and the railway unions, two groups that have tended not to see eye to eye on very much, come to us with a concern about the use of the investigators' reports of the statements taken by the Board investigators. They were worried that those could be used in disciplinary hearings between the company and the employee. They agreed that they should not be used, that they should remain confidential. The committee and the Government agreed with that change.
Many other amendments were put forward. I think the key is that we do have a better Bill. It is considerably better than what we started with. We learned a lot. Perhaps in three or four years when we get to the review process I and my colleague, the Member for Regina- Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin), will once again say "I told you so" as we find that something we had tried to do on Bill C-2, which was not accepted, actually would have made things better. However, that is the process we go through.

June 20, 1989
Accident Investigation
The only negative concern I have is that we did rush things a bit too much. We had a problem with regard to preparation of amendments because we wanted to find out what the Government was prepared to do in order that we would not duplicate effort. Because of that, some of the amendments we submitted were not translated into one of the official languages. That caused a delay and I can say in retrospect that we probably should have built that into the process to ensure that everything was presented to the committee at the same time and in the same way.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, as we did at second reading we will be supporting third reading of this Bill. It is a good day for transportation. I have not dealt with the issue of highway transport but I am sure my colleague will because it is an area of great interest to him. I look forward to seeing the new Board in place. I would encourage the Government to look carefully at who it appoints to this Board to ensure that it has the best possible people available and that they be appointed in a spirit of non-partisanship rather than using it as a resting place for tired old political war-horses. We need some good aviation, marine and rail individuals on this Board to take a good hard look at accident investigations in this country. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues on the Transport Committee for all their hard work.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us today government Bill C-2, an Act to establish the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board. At the outset there was some resistance by some Members of the esteemed Standing Committee on Transport during clause-by-clause consideration of the Board to not incorporate the word "safety" in the title of the Act. However, through the insistence of opposition Members we directed the Government's attention to the mandate of the Board, which is found in Clause 7, that is, that "the object of the Board is to advance transportation safety". The Government eventually saw the wisdom of our suggestion and, despite the committee chairman's observation that the title, in his words, "lacked sex appeal" or something very close to that, the TAIB or Transportation Accident Investigation Board was amended to include the word "safety".
I want to make it clear that I do not disagree with the intention of this Bill. In addition to aviation occurrences, the new Board will consolidate and be responsible for investigating occurrences in the modes of rail, marine, and pipelines transportation.
It must be noted that Bill C-2, when enacted, will replace CASB, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. That was a good idea. CASB did its job, conducting close to 700 investigations a year. It gained a solid reputation in aviation circles around the world. However, a grievous split developed in a most controversial case, Canada's worst air disaster, the crash of an Arrow Air chartered DC-8 at Gander, Newfoundland, in December, 1985, which claimed the lives of 248 U.S. soldiers and eight crew members.
Enter CASB. Four of nine board members, all of them intelligent, capable and knowledgeable, with full credentials, disagreed with the report of the Board which concluded that a thin layer of ice on the planes' wings was responsible for the crash. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) endorsed the report which then prompted the four dissenting members to call for public inquiries, not only into the controversial finding that icing caused Canada's worst air disaster, but into air traffic control problems as well.
In light of this and other problems, including the resignation of the Assistant Deputy Minister in charge of Canadian Aviation Safety, who resigned in the midst of controversy over the crash at Gander and the Air Ontario crash at Dryden, the Minister of Transport, instead of attempting to rectify problems that existed within CASB, chose to create a new board, virtually sweeping under the rug any outstanding questions in relation to Gander, Dryden and other problems the Government failed to deal with immediately in air transportation.
So we come to Bill C-2. While there are still many unanswered questions, are we guaranteed that this new Board will address them? Will Canadians ever get any answers? Although multi-modal in design, the new Board is entrusted with responsibilities and authority similar to those of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. Canadians are no more assured of increased safety now than they were in the past. There is nothing in Bill C-2 to prevent a repeat of the circumstances which led to the end of CASB.
What incredibly convenient timing, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Transport appoints an eminent outside authority, Mr. Justice Willard Estey, to review the Gander accident investigation and appoints Mr. Justice Virgil Moshansky to conduct an inquiry into the Dryden accident. However, before he is prepared to hear the reports from Estey or Moshansky, important information by the way which could be incorporated into this legislation, we find ourselves here today on a strict government timetable pushing Bill C-2 through the House of Commons.
June 20, 1989

On the subject of power, it was the contention of many witnesses who appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport that too much power will be handed to the chairman of the multi-modal board. Under Bill C-2 the chairman will have the power to hire and fire investigators, all the financial power, power to set the agenda, and the power to decide what Board members will do what work; all this power in the hands of a single individual. Let us not perpetuate the problems that existed under CASB where the powers were vested in one individual rather than in the Board as a whole. The chairman must be responsible to the Board.
In the overall scheme of things, the public lost its confidence in CASB because a group of Board members had to move out from under the umbrella of the Safety Board in order to publish their own minority report because a powerful chairman attempted to silence them. We can learn from this, Mr. Speaker. The very essence of democracy means to consider many points of view. We welcome and in fact look toward the divergence of opinion in order to judge effectively. Dissent is healthy. This House is a good example of that, Mr. Speaker. The multi-modal Board must make room for dissenting points of view and accept the variety of opinion. It all works toward ensuring that transportation, whether by air, rail, marine or pipeline, is as safe as it can be for all Canadians. That is the ultimate goal.
The Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), the chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport, is, I must say, a modest man. He speaks of co-operation and the spirit of constructive, non-partisan discussions which led us to this Bill. Well, aside from the cigar smoke, our effectiveness was fresh in its approach and a model for other committees to follow, due in large part, I might admit,, to the Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants.

I have also been through the experience of being summoned to a coroner's inquest. The railway lawyers and the Crown prosecutor took statements from us, interviewed us and cross-examined us on a witness stand.
I will never forget the instructions from the CPR lawyer from Montreal. This was in Calgary in the winter of, would you believe, Mr. Speaker, 1949-50.1 will never forget his instructions to us. Yet when I got that instruction, and I say to my good friend, the chairman of the Transport Committee, I wondered what would happen if I said some things which needed to be said. Then I realized if I did, I would be out of a job. I kind of liked the job. I worked hard at it and I was very conscientious about it. It was one of the reasons, I guess from my own background, why I was so concerned about Clause 24, for example.
I was concerned about statements taken from employees, and who they are taken by and what circumstances they are under because I have been there, damn it. I guess I kind of resented the expertise from legal eagles from the Department of Transport and some of the highly paid consultants and legal eagles who were there on behalf of a few of the witnesses we had. They have never had to do it.
It was the unanimous consensus of the committee in the first five minutes that this was the kind of legislation which we all wanted. One of the concerns we had was that this board must not only be independent but is seen to be. That was the problem which I and some of my colleagues had with Clause 24. I was very proud of the Railway Brotherhood which said they do not want any part of being sent a copy of the draft of the final report to comment on.
The Board should make its report without any comment from anybody. Once it has seen the evidence and heard from its investigators and once it has cross-examined witnesses and heard from the employer, the airline or railway, and have heard all the evidence, it makes its report. Every observer and participant in the hearings will have had his chance to have his say.
Once the Board has heard all the evidence, it makes a report and submits it to the Minister as specified in the Bill. Then if somebody disagrees with the findings of the Board, disagrees with evidence submitted by an investigator or any witness, he can go to the Minister and say: "We would like you to review the evidence". It is in the Bill. But you cannot have an airline, railroad, steamship company, a pipeline company, the Minister or any other Minister who has a direct interest in the matter-that could be the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) and a few others I could think of, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais)-making interventions on a draft report unless the Board will include those interventions and comments in its final report so that the public will know that this is a full and open public hearing. There will be nothing hidden and nothing secret. I still do not understand why the Government did not accept our Motion No. 10 at report stage, why it would not accept a similar amendment in the committee. It seems to me that it will come back to haunt us if at any time somebody can make some comments and send an intervention and a request to the board based on a draft of a final report.
June 20, 1989

Once it becomes publicly known that that intervention was made, particularly if it comes from a member of the Government even if the board totally ignores that intervention, the integrity, independence and openness of the board is in question. Why we are passing an otherwise good Bill that leaves that possibility there in the legislation passes all understanding. Why the stubbornness of the Government on this item is beyond me completely. Why would a Minister of any integrity, honesty and reputation even want to have the opportunity? At least the Railway Brotherhood said: "We don't want any draft report. We will have our chance with the observers that we have at the scene of the accident or incident. We will have an observer at all the hearings. We will have all our opportunities to make our representation to protect our members. We don't want access to a draft of the final report".
This one item in this Bill flies in the face of the bitter experience we had with previous accident investigation boards. The Elon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Keyes) raised the matter about the CASB. When he mentioned Hamilton I thought to myself, let's not dredge that up again.

The matter had to do with air traffic control, the safety issue and inspection of aircraft. We did it when we came to deregulation. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre was the guy who started it. He became Minister of Transport because his predecessor was against deregulation. What we have done with the laws in Canada is to force otherwise honest and reputable companies to cut comers. They have no choice when the bottom line is what tells the tale. If you have a jet engine that should be overhauled after 2,000 hours, well, we hear it said let's go 2,500 hours. In 99.9 per cent of the time you would get away with it. I am rising today because I have received new and additional information since I spoke in the House the last time. I agree with the intent of this Bill which establishes the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board, but I do not agree with the hidden agenda behind it. The hidden agenda is to cover up the truth about the cause of the accident in Gander which killed 258 American soldiers.
The other hidden agenda behind this Bill is to dismantle the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, the members of which are doing an excellent job now. As we know, five members of the board submitted their report stating that the cause of the accident was icing on the wings while four members of the board with the highest qualifications in aeronautics in Canada submitted a minority report stating that it was not caused by icing on the wings but was caused by some explosion or other force.
June 20, 1989

Last night I saw colour pictures taken the day after the accident. A helicopter had followed the path of the plane that crashed taking pictures every step of the way. If you saw those pictures, Mr. Speaker, you would see that there was no indentation in the ground where the plane crashed. If the crash was caused by icing on the wings, then as the plane came down, there would have been a gouge in the earth. There is no such indentation in the earth. The pictures show small fragments of the airplane scattered all over the bush. Trees are clipped off from where the plane first started coming in, but there is a row of trees standing while parts of the plane are scattered all over. The only way those parts could get there is if the plane somehow disintegrated in the air and came falling down. One part of the plane has a gaping hole in it. The picture clearly shows that this hole was caused by some explosion, not by icing on the wings.
I would not feel right, having been sent here by my constituents, knowing this information and not sharing it in the House. I share it now before the Bill leaves this House. I know it is going to the Senate and I urge the Senate to conduct a full investigation before giving the Bill Royal Assent. The Senate has the power to call in additional witnesses who were not called under the previous investigation. I invite the Senate to look at the pictures I saw last night and I think it will probably come to the same conclusion to which I came which is that Mr. Justice Estey should be given full powers to reopen the investigation and hear witnesses who were not called before. Then and only then should we pass Bill C-2.
I was the Parliamentary Secretary who passed the Canadian Aviation Safety Bill, Bill C-163. In the debate at that time, we felt we should go with a unimodal safety board and iron out the kinks before we brought in a multimodal board. The Government has not demonstrated that it can manage the nine members of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. The Minister accepted the report of the five and immediately ordered a secret investigation into air safety. Why did he do that if he believed the report? I highlight that I agree with the intent of the Bill. I do not agree with the two hidden agendas of the Bill. I invite the Senate to do a full investigation before giving approval.

My concerns are compounded

Some people would like the Senate to give this Bill more consideration. I commend my colleague, the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) for expressing the concerns that he has expressed and through the public record, through Hansard, he has requested that the Senate give this Bill some serious consideration. However, I see other flaws in the legislation.
While Members consider passing this Bill, and Members have stood up and complimented one another on how great it was to deal with it in the spirit of non-partisanship, I would submit that there have been some oversights that ought to be addressed. At the very least, I would like to discharge my responsibilities by putting my comments on the record. Hopefully, again, the Senate will consider my submissions and the submissions of any other Member in its deliberations on Bill C-2.
To get to the point with respect to my concerns, we know that the purpose of the Bill is to establish a new board to investigate accidents in Canada. That is fair enough. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board had a lot of problems over the last number of years. It embarrassed the Government on a number of occasions with respect to the Gander crash and the near misses at Pearson International Airport. There was a need for a more comprehensive board or commission. That is fine.
Clause 3 tries to define the purpose of the Bill, or how the Bill applies. Specifically, I will only address the situation of air disasters, when there are crashes involving aircraft. Clause 3(1) states:
This Act applies in respect of aviation occurrences-
The clause goes on to describe three situations to which the Bill applies. First, it is when the occurrences happen in or over Canada, including the international waters of Canada and the territorial sea of Canada. That is pretty straightforwrd. If an airplane crash occurs somewhere in Canada or within Canadian jurisdiction, then this Bill applies to that particular crash.

That, presumably, refers to a foreign Government which can say to the Board which is established by this Bill: "We want you to investigate. Come in and investigate".

Mr. Speaker, on June 91 questioned the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) on the status of water and soil conservation accords and agreements with the Provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. My question was a follow-up to one asked by my colleague, the Member for Regina-Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. de Jong) on May 3. At that time the Minister stated that the agreement with Saskatchewan had not been signed because certain criteria had to be satisfied. However he did not specify exactly what these criteria were. The other possibility is that the Minister is not being factual with the House and in that case there is some underlying reason which has not been made clear to the House. I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to explain if that is the case. I find both of these possibilities hard to accept but I ask the Parliament Secretary to please tell this House and the people of Canada which one it is.
I would also like to know to what criteria the Minister is referring. They must be very important criteria since in the case of Saskatchewan he has had five months to study the agreement and the criteria. It appears to be criteria so important that no one seems to know exactly what the criteria are, criteria so important that the provinces do not know about them. Criteria so important that his own staff does not seem to know about them, criteria so important that perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary himself does not know about them.
June 20, 1989

I do trust, however, that since the Minister has seen fit to send the Parliamentary Secretary to the House to answer the question he has taken time at least to brief him on these criteria. I am beginning to wonder whether the Minister himself knows what the criteria is to which he is referring. I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to please explain to this House what criteria the Minister referred to in his answers of May 3 and June 3.
I trust and hope that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary will not take the arrogant approach which has become a trademark of the Government and not answer this part of my question.
Finally, I and many people across this great land would like to know when these four agreements are going to be signed by the Minister. The Government speaks in glowing terms of the environment, it says that the environment is an important part of its mandate and an important part of the work that it is going to perform over the next four years. Certainly soil and water conservation is an integral and important part of the environment. If this is an example of how the Government is going to act with respect to the environment, Canadians should be warned that the commitment to the environment which the Government pretends to have is nothing more than an elaborate fraud.
Every region of this nation needs soil and water conservation accords from potato farmers in Prince Edward Island to wheat growers in Alberta. Typical are the residents in the Outlook area in my own riding who need some assistance from either the provincial or the federal Government in this important area.
In conclusion, I will simply reiterate my points. First, why is the Minister stating that there are negotiations going on while, at the same time, his staff is denying it? Second, to what criteria was the Minister referring in his answers of May 3 and June 9? Third, when will these agreements be signed? Those are three simple questions, the answers to which are very important to the future of this nation.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the concern expressed by the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Laporte) on federal-provincial soil conservation efforts. There is a growing sense of urgency among Canadians that we must act to protect our soil and water resources in order to ensure the long-term viability and prosperity of our agriculture and food industry.
The Government of Canada and the provinces have agreed to work together to safeguard these resources. This commitment was spelled out in the National Agricultural Strategy signed by the federal and provincial Ministers of Agriculture in 1986.
The National Agricultural strategy calls for a co-ordinated soil and water conservation program adapted to meet the particular needs of each province. It was agreed that the program should include awareness and education programs, improved extension, technical and advisory services, more on-site demonstrations of conservation techniques and additional research.
In December, 1987, the federal Government responded with the National Soil Conservation Program that made funds available for a new nation-wide push to conserve and improve Canadian farmland. This three-year, $150 million co-operative effort between the federal Government and the provinces will encourage long-term soil conservation measures.
As envisioned in the National Agriculture Strategy, the program will involve on-farm technical and financial assistance, demonstrations, research and monitoring.
This approach recognizes that it is the farmer who is on the front line of the soil conservation battle. The program will also work to increase public awareness about the need to conserve our soils.
Program components will be tailored to reflect the nature and extent of problems in each region. Federal funding will be distributed based on the extent of soil degradation problems and the availability of matching funds in each province.
June 20,1989

Adjournment Debate
The federal Government has successfully reached basic soil and water accords with the provinces. These accords give us a framework for future consultation and planning on all agriculture soil and water issues.
We are now working on actual agreements for soil conservation activities under the national soil conservation program. We are also working out the financial and administrative arrangements with each province.
Negotiations have taken place with the provinces. The Hon. Member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre has expressed his particular concern about the agreement with Saskatchewan.
In the case of Saskatchewan and the other western provinces, factors such as last year's drought had to be taken into consideration and changes made to the original proposals.
We have done that, and we expect the agreement with Saskatchewan to be concluded in the very near future. This Government recognizes the importance of conserving our soils. Once the agreements are signed, we are prepared to move quickly to put in place the national soil conservation program.
AIRPORTS-CANADIAN AVIATION SAFETY BOARD RECOMMENDATIONS/AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS

Mr. Speaker, I intervene this evening due to my growing frustration over this Government's inability and its unwillingness to respond to the safety deficiencies at Pearson International Airport.
I am here to pursue a question which I asked on April 5, 1989. It is absurd that after a full two months, we are still waiting for this Government to address in an effective manner, the safety problems at Pearson Airport.
An article in the Globe and Mail on June 1, 1989, entitled, "Making Canada's Airports Safe" said that: "A lack of safety in air traffic control is being blamed for near collisions at Toronto's Pearson Airport". The article goes on to say: "-the safety problem at Canada's largest airport, like the problem that plagues other major Canadian airports, boils down to economics-Airline deregulation, with the major opportunities it has provided for lower air fares and significant increases in airline travel, this deregulation has posed no problem for the private sector. Private suppliers have provided more planes, more in flight meals, more stewardesses, more pilots and more fuel to respond to the increased demand for air travel. However, no corresponding expansion has occurred in the supply of airport facilities-" This is a failing of this Government, Mr. Speaker.
I informed this House two months ago that a Department of Transport document clearly outlined in June, 1987, that the Government totally failed to make adequate effects on airline deregulation. More specifically, I advised the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) on April 5 that Canadian travellers cannot afford to play Russian roulette with air passenger safety. I asked the Minister: "What are you doing about controllers at Pearson so that the safety of Canadian air travellers can be assured?" This Government has a very difficult time in answering questions about air safety. Every time I have made an intervention in this House, I have been given a response relating to air traffic delays. It is precisely because I do understand the difference between safety deficiencies and air traffic delays that I continue to raise this issue, obviously in vain.
The Minister of Transport, for example, responded to my question saying: "People who are surprised at the delays at Pearson should understand that the directives are quite clear. We handle the number of flights that our air traffic controllers can handle". Delays, Mr. Speaker, are a symptom of the unsafe condition. There are not enough air traffic controllers at Pearson.
If conditions at Pearson were safe, we would not have experienced the three misses, one on December 20 and two on January 10, which happened within three hours of each other.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that time is running on. It is half past the hour. It has been a long day. Let me just close by saying that perhaps the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary may wish to explain to Canadian air travellers why this Government, in light of its self proclaimed commitment to safety, has chosen to reduce funding to air traffic control services by $3,575,000, or 67 person-years as outlined on page 2-57 of the 1989-90 Transport Department estimates for this year.
June 20, 1989

Is this an example of this Government's commitment to safety? If it is, we are in serious trouble. In light of these facts, will this Government stop giving Canadian air travellers false assurances? Will this Government undertake to inform air travellers using Pearson International Airport that there are safety deficiencies that do exist? It is their duty and obligation to do this.

OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY-CLOSURE OF CENTRE-GOVERNMENT POSITION-RIGHT OF CANADIANS TO INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first came to the House I heard Members talking about the late show. Now I know what they mean.
I rise pursuant to a question I asked on June 13 regarding the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety. In reply to my question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Corbeil) regarding the federal Government's elimination of funding for the centre by April 1, 1991, I was told that the centre would not close.
This, in my opinion, is difficult to believe given this Government's fiscal plan for the centre. Unless the centre becomes self-financing by 1992, it will in all likelihood be forced to close.
At the present time the federal Government contributes approximately $8 million a year to the centre's operations. For the fiscal year 1989-90 the funding for the centre has been cut by $1.5 million. This is only the beginning. In 1990-91 the funding will be furthered reduced by $4.6 million and by April 1, 1991 the centre will be entirely cut off from federal funding. This certainly puts the centre's survival into question and the good useful work of the centre, as described by the Minister of Labour, in jeopardy.
The centre was created in order to promote the fundamental right of Canadians to a healthy and safe working environment by creating a national institute concerned with the study, encouragement and co-operative advancement of occupational health and safety. Since the centre's inception in 1978, the centre has done just that by providing the Canadian workforce with valuable information regarding work place hazards.

June 20, 1989
Adjournment Debate
The centre's statistics are impressive. In 1988-89 alone, the centre answered by phone and mail over
26,000	requests from individuals for occupational health and safety information. Its newsletter had an international following of over 35,000 readers and it distributed over 350,000 publications in response to requests.
These statistics represent the fact that the centre is providing a useful service to Canadians. In the wake of its increasing popularity, the Government has introduced unprecedented cuts to the centre's funding with the goal of self-sufficiency by April, 1991. In keeping with this, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Corbeil) has asked the President and Chief Executive Officer of the council to produce a plan for alternative funding for the centre.
There are funding alternatives that have been presented so that the centre will not be forced to shut down come April, 1991. The centre could raise money through fund-raising projects, from a capital loan from the Government, by charging for present services, from provincial grants or through assimilation into a federal Department. The Minister has, however, ruled out federal funding, charges to ordinary users and assimilation into Labour Canada. None of the funding alternatives which have been proposed could alone meet the financial needs of the centre.
Given the alarming statistics regarding occupational health and safety in Canada, we know there is indeed a need for the services provided by the centre. Over
800,000	work days are lost annually by Canadians due to disabling injuries and over 440 lives are lost yearly due to industrial accidents. It is as a result of this that over $7 billion is spent annually to cover medical expenses, compensation for lost earnings, pensions, insurance and loss of production.
These statistics are disturbing. How can the Government justify these cuts, particularly since it has made such a strong contribution to the cause of Canadian workers only to leave them with absolutely nothing? Workers deserve Government action in eliminating occupational hazards in the workplace. In this vein, the Canadian Occupational Health and Safety Centre must continue as an independent national tripartite organization.
The centre provides a necessary service to Canadian workers and should extend this information service, not have it curtailed by fiscal restraint. In the meantime, alternative funding mechanisms should be investigated so that some products could be developed in order to increase revenues. These mechanisms should not, however, be permitted to impair the reliability of the centre's information work or the flow of information to the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety. Canadians have a right to this information and they should get it. What is the Government's intention for the health and safety of Canadian workers and for the future of the centre?

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY-CLOSURE OF CENTRE-GOVERNMENT POSITION-RIGHT OF CANADIANS TO INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to reassure the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. Proud) and this House that the planned reductions in the funding of the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety will not result in the closing of the centre. The reductions merely reflect the Government's belief that the centre is now a viable enterprise capable of becoming more financially self-sufficient. The centre has already demonstrated that it is able to recover some of its costs. In the last fiscal year, for example, it recovered $440,000 while in this fiscal year it plans to recover $1,400,000. I have no doubt that the centre can earn even more of its income from its operations.
For 11 years since its creation in 1978, the centre has been provided with the financial support it needed to establish itself and to develop a variety of useful information services. Today, the centre is able to provide a full range of services. They range from technical bulletins to a set of compact discs containing volumes of information on every aspect of occupational safety and health. This latter product is called a CCINFO disc. It is an innovative use of compact disc technology which has received international attention.
I am convinced that most of its clients, especially corporate ones, are prepared to pay the centre for the true value of creating these and other products. Although the centre will have to charge for its products, I want to assure this House that all Canadian workers will be able to receive the information they need through their employers to do their jobs safely. Please allow me to explain.
June 20, 1989

The Pan-Canadian workplace hazardous materials information system and other federal, provincial and territorial occupational safety and health legislation gives workers the right to be informed of the hazards associated with their jobs. It is the duty of employers to provide their employees with this information. This legislated requirement will provide the centre with a considerable market for its information services.
Adjournment Debate
In closing, I believe that the planned reductions in the centre's funding will neither close it down nor deprive Canadian workers of essential information.
